many another city chap-he ,ad loved

Gradually Dan Wales renewed his WOO
ing of Ruth, and by June their wedding
day was set. Dan knew that he did not
possess Ruth's entire heart, but he was
confident of winning 1t in the end.


1t was a beautiful day late in June
when Ruth Fielding stood In her bridal
attire before ner simple dressing table.


1t was a paIa. thoughtful face that con-
fronted her in the mirror. Suddenly she
went to her bed and knelt praying that
God would help her forget her faithless
lover ard increase her love for Dan, AMI
that she might make him a loving wife.


While she knelt the door opened and
Eva White. dressed to attend the we'd
ding. peered in and then entered softly.
locked the door and went and dropped to
her knees beside Ruth.


"Oh. Ruth. pray for me. too" she
sobbed wildly Forgive me II you can
1 have wronged you!"


With their arms around each other.
Puth heard Eva Whites confession. ThS
package of suppressed letters-there were
eight Of them in Barry's bold writing
all unopened, besides the single letter
Ruth had sent to him.


And the letters. Ruth read them with
streaming eyes Barry had been faithful
His parents would welcome her with open
arms. Barry now believed Ruth to have
been the faithless one. She had returned
his ring and he had never received
letter from her. While they talked. Mrs
Fielding brought the smiling bridegroom
to see his bride-and In their presence
Eva White repeated her amazing confess
sion.


Fifteen minutes later. Dan Wales
white and grim looking. went down and
dismissed the wedding guests and the
astonished minister.


Indefinitely postponed" he told them
all. When he was alone he went to the
telephone and called Barry Lane on the
long distance wire.


In Seaport they still talk about that
June day. How the wedding was post
poned how Barry Lane and his parents
came racing down in an automobile. and
how Dan Wales went after the minister
again. and the odd change Of bridegrooms
at the eleventh hour.


They tell about the marriage in the
Fielding house, and add that Barry Lane
was the happy bridegroom. while Dan
White was best man and Eva White was
the brides attendant


In the end Dan married Eva White,
and out of the sin and pride and pain OF
that bitter year came quiet happiness

Reports here indicate that the occupa-
ton of tho seaside of the Gallipoli penin-
sula by the Allies is virtually complete.
The British forces on the European side
have defeated, with heavy losses, every
attempt by the Turks to turn them back
on their ships. The casualties among the
Turks In killed and wounded number
10000, and many prisoners have been
made. Gallipoli and Maidas were seized.


British forces that effected a landing
near Enos, on the Aegean Sea, at point
where the Turkish line approaches the
Bulgarian frontier. are moving In south
easterly direction In an attempt to throw
line of positions across the eastern end
of the Gallipoli peninsula and thus cut
off all the Turkish land forces on that
tongue of land. They are reported to
have advanced 20 miles in the last five
days.


The British have intrenched their vari-
GUS bases and are slowly feeling out the
fortified positions along the peninsula
The heaviest fighting has taken place in
the territory between Cape Suvla and
the southern extremity of the peninsula.
There the Turks had strongly intrenched
themselves, utilizing entanglements and
masked pits, but the big guns of the
warships smashed the traps and opened
the way for the British advance.


On the Asiatic side the French troops
are progressing along the lines planned
and in every way are cooperating with
the British 1t is stated here that the
French have captured more than 5000
Turkish prisoners.


Following the all-day bombardment
Wednesday of the forts the heavier ships
of the allied fleet remained in the straits
all night and resumed the bombardment
Thursday. 1t is stated here that num-
ber of the Turkish batteries in the vein
ity of Karantina have been silenced. The
prisoners taken on the European side are
being sent to Tenedos.

approaching wave of prosperity through

dieting a profound depression then. Let
the "shorts" take heart. Everything comes

Bud. Baker and Richard OBrien, two
Washington boys, who motored to the
Pacific expositions on an Indian motor
cycle five months ago, are expected to
arrive in the National Capital tomor-
row at noon.


When they arrive in this city tomor-
row they will have covered 10000 miles
and have been away exactly five months
to the hour. The machine is still
equipped with the original set of tires
which were on the machine when they
left Washington. They motored through
twenty states on the westward trip and
twenty-five on the homeward- bound
journey.


Both of the boys are well, according
to information. received by The Star
a few days ago, and have suffered very
few hardships since leaving their
homes. They have lost about ten
pounds each in weight. After visiting
their relatives here they will return to
Springfield, Mass, where they have
been appointed to positions with the
manufacturers Of the Indian machine.

A place where comradeship, con-
tentment, and freedom unite to form
that mighty power. community spirit
such is Camp Good Will For com
\ munity spirit is not a myth at this
| summer outing camp of the Asso-
ciated Charities. Here Servians, AUS
| TRANS. Russians, Germans. Irish, Scots.
Italians, Syrians and Americans all
learn the meaning of comradeship,
and later. friendship.


Twelve years ago. Commodore Da-
venport took small group Of boys
| from Noel House on a camping trip.
| That started the summer camps. Now.
| Camp Good viii is beginning its
eleventh season. The Baby Hospital
Camp has three years to its credit.
and Camp Pleasant. the colored camp.
! four.


All during July and August. groups
of 100 children and mothers who other
wise never would see the country
spend two happy weeks at Camp
| Good Will.


Children Shy at First.
Wednesday. June 80. was the open
| ing day Long before the appointed
time Wednesday morning, the campers
began to gather at Neighborhood
House. the starting point From there
automobiles carried them to the camp.
where the camp superintendent, her


six trained helpers, and eight VOL
unteer workers greeted each arriving
party. The mothers were glad to rest
in the shady pavilion and soon were
talking together. The children were
shy at first, but led by those who
! had been before" they became in
terested in the see-saws. swings. and
sand pile. and by dinner time were
friends with the camp and all 1t con-
tains.


At twelve o'clock a bugle gave the
signal for lines to be formed. and all
marched in to the first camp meal in
the big community dining room. The
camp prayer which preceded the meal
is truly American:


For peace and for plenty. for freedom, for rest.
For Iog in the land from the east to the west


For the dear starry flag with its red. white. and blue
We thank Thee from hearts that tender and
true.


After dinner, tents were assigned.
baggage unpacked, and the campers
were "at home


The camp consists of forty tents
loaned by the government, a dining
porch with kitchen ATTACHED. a covered
pavilion, a frame house fer the SUI
perintendent- and her assistants. ano
the barn and stables. Awnings and
screens on the pavilion and dining
hall. and wooden flooring for .he tents
add to the general comfort of the
campers Back of the grounds is the
vegetable garden which furnishes all
the vegetables for the table Last wear
the garden was so successful that
vegetables were shared with .he Baby
Hospital Camp, across the road.
Everything Up-to-date.


Everything is as up-to-date as the
limited funds of the Associated Chari-
ties can make it. The camp even boasrs
a drinking fountain! Besides the reg
ular Waterman a mounted policeman
visits the camp daily and brings mail
from Brightwood. And always the
American flag. promising liberty and
protection to all under its folds waves
from the top of a fifty-foot staff.


Every morning. first the girls. and
then the boys, go swimming in the
creek. From 3 to IL the little children
learn songs, stories. and games: while
the older ones are taught playground
work, including basketry, crocheting,
sewing and games of all kinds. A di-
rector supported by the Playground
Association, assisted by six volunteer
boy scouts, has charge of the boys.
The girls are taught by the regular
camp workers. Some days there are
walks and drives through Rock Creek
Park And there are gala days when
the Navy Yard Band plays it's best
for the children. At other times a
graphophone and piano furnish music
On special days. too. plays, recita-
tions, games. and races vary the reg
ular program. From $50 in the morn
ing until o'clock at night the days
are full at Camp Good Will.


Besides having good time, the
girls and boys learn the lesson of neat
ness Each one learns to make his own
bed: and on the days when all the beds
of tent are perfectly made that tent
wears an American flag. The boys also
take charge of keeping the grounds in
good condition.


Three Clubs in Camp.


There are three Camp Good viii
clubs: Mothers Club, Boys Club, and
Girls Club. Each person who comes to
the camp joins one of these groups
At first, the clubs were only temper
airy, but the members passed a unani-
nous vote to continue the meetings
during the winter. So now the clubs
are fixed institutions of the camp life,
and afterwards, of the city life. The
Mothers Club has sixty-seven menu
bers. the Boys Club 102. and the Girls
Club 14S.


Here is the pledge Of the Mothers
Club-a pledge perfect: I'VE are happy
in Gods greatest gift, Mother Love,
and will be true to our trust


The camp might well be called the
most beautiful spot around Washing
ton-and also the coolest. Everywhere
are shade trees, and all about the hills
of Rock Creek Park, with the ragged
outline of the trees against the sky
line. 1t is an ideal camping ground.
and therefore, it is not strange that
joy is contagious. that every ono is
happy, and that every one wears q
smile. Camp Good Will itself is cure
for the blues.


Across the road from Camp Good
Will is the Baby Hospital Camp, a life
saving station for babies under two
years Here a trained force consisting
of a superintendent, resident doctor.
three trained nurses, and four maids
care for fourteen of the city's sickest
babies, and in almost every case with
complete success. There is no limit to
stay at Baby Hospital Camp; and
while the babies are gaining strength
with proper treatment. the mothers
are learning how to keep them well
after leaving camp.

Milan, Aug. 22-A A crippled Italian
submarine burst through the surface
of the Adratic to-oay, after a sew
enty-two-hour su5mersion. In the
foul air pent up inside of her lay her
captain, dead, with three Of his crew.
Two more men died as, her weakened
engines scarcely turning, she lurched
toward the rendezvous Of the Italian
feet


Men of the warsnips looked at the
craft in bewilderment as she slipped
alongside. 1t looked ike the Neroid,
reported sunk three days before by
the Austrians. Then, when they real
lied that it was really that vessel. a
great roar Of cheering went up from
their decks. The vessel given up for
lost had returned


Tonight all Italy is thrilling with
the terror that the crew Of damaged
submarine, unable to rise from the
bottom of the Adriatic, might have felt
and did not feel. For three whole
days thirty men groped about in the
foul air of their submarine prison,
without light, without food, without
even sufficient oxygen to breathe. Then
when hope seemed lost, when the cap
tain and three seamen had died, the
blindly searching fingers cf the engi-
neer touched the break in the connec-
tions which had crippled the engines
and the Nereid shot TO the surface.


In part, the Austrian report o. the
submarines sinking was true. A tor
pedo was launched at her and she did
20 to the bottom. The torpedo did not
find its mark, however. The Italian
commander saw the trail of bubbles
rushing toward him. He jerked fran
tically at the diving lever, and the
vessel plunged, deep ard swift. over
her back the death bolt passed, but the
Nereid did not rise from her dive. With
her lights snuffed out, with her en-
gines dead, She slowly sank to the bot
tom Of the ocean, and lay there with
thirty men inside her.


There was only the thinnest shred Of
hope. but the entombed men grasped
this coolly. II the break in the engine
could be found they might rise TO the
surface again. And in the blaekest
darkness they set out 10 find it. The
air grew foul, but they still crawled
about, feeling desperately Men began
to drop, but the few who could move
groped on. Then after three days sub
mersion the Nereid began TO rise. The
matches were flung open, and clean
sea air rushed into ner foul interior.


"The Nereid, sunk. Is risen again"
is the message that telegraph aad
wireless are flashing to every Italian
tonight.

Forty-one Western railroads are now
arguing before the Interstate Commerce
Commission for an increase in freight
rates. Their case does not differ greatly
from that of the Eastern railroads
which obtained relief from the commits
sion last December. The Western roads
have not been as hard hit by industrial
depression as the Eastern roads have
been. But they have the same story to
tell-increased investment in plant and
equipment, larger cost of operation and
steadily falling income. Moreover, the
financial arrangements due 10 the Euro
pean war compel all carriers which bor-
row money to borrow it at higher rates.


The Interstate Commerce Commission
brought itself reluctantly to the point Of
recognizing in the Eastern freight rate
case that regulation must work both
ways. The authority Of the commission
had been used for years to lower rates
and restrict earnings. Wage arbtra-
tons. higher state and federal taxes and
safety first legislation were all working
TO The same end, and when hard times
and the European war came along the
carriers were left struggling against
ruinous combination of adverse in
huences. The commission, after refus-
ing the Eastern increase, yielded to pub
lie opinion and reversed itself. 1t is on
the right road now in admitting that the
unjust balance against the carriers must
be righted, not alone in their interest,

Dallas, Tex. Aug. 16.-Full effects of
the terrific West Indian hurricane
which passed through the Yucatan
Channel Sunday were felt at Gulf coast
points late to-day. when the wind
reached a velocity of seventy miles an
hour. Alarm was felt for the safety
Of various ports, notably Galveston,
concerning which disturbing reports
were circulated.


Telegraph wires 20 the port went
down at $50 tonight. The last mes
sage said:


"The tropical storm which struck
Galveston to-day, while very severe,
had caused no serious damage or loss
Of life up to 6 o'clock this evening.


"The Galveston sea wall, built as a
precaution against such hurricanes,
withstood the fury of the storm and
showed no signs Of weakening. The
storm struck the city late in the fore
noon at a velocity of thirty-four miles
an hour.


At 8 o'clock tonight the highest We
locity averaged 65 to 73 miles an hour,



heavy rain tell throughout the day and
tonight the streets are filled with
water to the curbing.


II was estimated that five thousand
persons left Galveston during the last
thirty-six hours. Practically all homes
on the beach had been evacuated and
the hfesaving crew was held in readl-
ness. The city was in darkness to-
night.


Rising tides which flooded the rail-
road between Sabine and Port Arthur
were reported at Beaumont to have
trapped two women and three men at
Sabine. The women refused to leave
after all other inhabitants had de-
serted the town. Other coast resorts,
including Port Bolivar, Caplen and
Follower. were reported under water


Galveston's isolation caused the
greatest anxiety in the rest OF the
state. However. the fact that the wind
at o'clock was blowing from the
north and that the water, which had
backed into the streets, was from the
bay side of the island tonight led
those who are familiar with the geo
graphical position of the city and the
history Of its storms to entertain new
hopes that the gale would not result IN
a disaster.

Just now many new travellers coming for
ward. They frankly declare that they would like
to destroy all the old trails. They say many in
terestng and clever and even brilliant things. They
show that some of our most popular trails were
created by folly But they forget that if we were
to destroy all the trails the weaknesses that
have expressed human nature since the beginning
new trails. To hear them talk, might think
that they were the only tra-makers that had ever
come into being that they alone could give sure
guidance. They patronize and sneer at the old
trail-makers. They speak if they had some
direct communication with the Divine But they
lack, as they proudly show, the divinest Of all
mentioned in their presence, they would laugh.
Self-conhdence is their note, sustained with arro-
gance.

There many who arc trying TO create new
trails. Some of them show great courage. They
know that they are destined to suffer. But they
arc willing. They really care less for themselves
than for those that are to follow. They are none
the less admirable because, occasionally hap
pens, their trails lead into bog where they them
selves perish. 1t is not success alone that counts
The best of any enterprise is whatever generosity
may lie in it, whatever unselfshness. On the
other hand, there are the trail-makers that arc
merely wilful and selfish. The mere sight of
trail may cause them to wish to take another di-
rection. The accumulated guidance of the past
they like to throw over contemptuously. They
know better. Even when they find themselves lost
with despair in their eyes, they may not learn the
lesson, so blinded they with their conceit and
vanity.

The problem of legibility of humber

strated that the most legible color

blnations were adopted in Iowa, where

To the Editor Of The Tribune.


Sir: Suffragists agree with the women
Of Europe that the present war could not
have been averted, also that a different
sentiment may be made to grow for the
future.


In view Of the fact that women will edu-
cate the next generation, Miss Florence
Shumway now advises them to devote their
entire energy to this task, and cease their
futile efforts for votes" Women are con-
cededly the less belligerent sex, and they
should without doubt educate the future
generation toward peaceful sentiments.
Nevertheless, working for votes is effective
and constructive work.


The ballot Is known to be the quickest
and most efficient means Of expressing the
opinions of the individual. Through vot-
ing women Immediately exercise en- inhu-
ence, while in training the young they
have TO wait years for a result, then per-
haps only to find that their influence has
been nil. LINDA L. CONTENT.

The boy was noticed by the telephone

clerk, Matthew Rogers, who compared

ing newspaper stories. Rogers spoke
to Goodhue, who was incapable OF max
ing a coherent answer. They notified
the Police Department. and Detective
Sergeant James Ward took the young
man in charge, notifying his father at

Young Goodhue was taken to the col

nourishment. He slept while and

Symington, Of New York City, that
the last he remembered was going into
a lunch room the night he disappeared.


DR.. Harry Arnold regards the case as
one OF genuine amnesia and thinks that
the young man will soon completely
recover. Hard work in preparation for
a scholarship examination caused IN
somnia the last three weeks. he Is
believed to have spent most Of the time
since Sunday walking. He had been
several hours in the Garde lobby.

q member Of the Alpha Delta Phi fra
ternlty.

mans mother, was informed BY. his

but had not complained of the din,

"Archangel is the only city in this
region whose name is known in the out
side world, and the only place that has
been able to achieve an individual dis
tinction in the midst of the vastness,
the desolation and the congealing
winters of Russia's north. There is
much economic value in the north, the
forests are filled with valuable fur
bearing animals. the lower forests are
rich in noble trees. the higher forests
in pitch and tar. the tundras in rein
deer herds, and great sturgeon are
caught through the ice of the rivers.
which produce large quantities of this
delicate fish meat and caviar.


The English established a trading
factory near present Archangel, dur
since their coming the region has been
exploited by pioneers. by adventurous
traders, trappers. huntsmen and fisher
men, but the country has never passed
the pioneer stage. The roads. for the
most part. are barely marked trails,
narrow, unleveled ribbons through
vast forests, indfferently corduroyed
caussways through swamp and marsh
lands and uncertain tracks through the
northern tundra. Post stations are
scattered over the governments far
apart. where hardy little horses and
prehistoric types of conveyances are
kept for the occasional trader, the oc-
casonal letter and the rare visitor
The villages are small and poor and
forgetful of the modern world and all
that it contains. Between them are
leagues of solitude.
headline: Archangel the Only City.

Winter sports are so delightful that
only the cold-blooded woman who likes
to sit by the fire and spin fails to take
an interest In them Skating. toboggan>
ing, motoring. golf on fine days, walking,
skiing and various other sports have
many advocates. Even II one cannot az

forms Of winter exercise, one can at least
make point OF walking regularly.


Suitable clothes, even for the winter
walk, are essential No one is more mis-
erably uncomfortable than the woman
for a winter stroll. Fortunately fashion
this winter fayors warm clothes-high-
necked coats, long-cleeved coats, skirted
coats and full, protecting skirts Even
high shoes or spats are essential to the
fashionable woman. and all these details
make for comfortable warmth.


Sweaters, however. will always remain
the chief friend of the woman who loves
the air. They are especially pretty this
year, knitted in gay silks, with scarfs
and sashes and caps to match, and for
heavier wear those of angora wool are
decidedly attractive. There are some
new ones with plaid and striped knitted
silk collars and cuffs and revers that are
in good style.


The woman who knows how to knit or
crochet may well make sweater, cap and
mufher or sash for herself, either in wool
or silk. Directions for making them can
be had in booklets at the worsted counter
in almost any shop, and the work Is
pleasant and certainly satisfactory in its
results.

they failed to notice the lowering clouds.

but before the second came Coxswain
Allan McLane headed the frail shell

with all their raight. Nickalls stood by
In the coaching launch and saw them
safely started on their way, and then
went to the rescue Of the sophomore
class crew. which was flve miles out in
the harbor when the storm arose.

them. They were having all they could
do to make headway against the waves.
which grew higher every moment. G.
v. Caesar. Of Tacoma, Wash. was near
by In a single scull, which he managed
to keep r!ghtsd with difficulty. With
the coaching launch as a protection

more rapid. Caesar was taken into the

while the eight-oared crew stayed with
Its she'll After a hard tussle against

cove. their boat full of water. There

There is much sound reasoning in the


plea for simple diet. And in spring,


especially, every housekeeper should


make an effort to simplify the diet of


the family she caters to. For in spring,


when an abundance of fresh vegeta bles


begin to come into the markets, when


the system Graves refreshing, rich and


spicy foods are a mistake. In the win


ter they seem sometimes necessary;


certainly they appeal to the winter pal
ate But the very fact that the spring


palate Graves crisp and fresh foods


shows that the heavier ones are out
of place at this season


For breakfast. fruit should always


form a part Of the spring diet Oranges


and apples are not SO easy to get at


this season, and berries and other sum


mer fruits are not yet here. but prunes
steamed figs and dates, cooked apples,
stewed rhubarb and occasionally good
oranges can be found Fried ca kes
spring dietary. Crisp buttered toast
and light mullins are in keeping with
the season. Eggs and broiled bacon
should take the place of meats


Fish should be used frequently for
dinner in place of meat, and one fresh
vegetable should be served at dinner
every day-tomatoes. spinach, young
carrots, green onions. sliced Bermuda
onions young cabbage carefully cook
ed, stewed lettuce, asparagu tboiled


creamed), radishes, string beans, boiled
onions. and any other fresh. green
vegetable. Salads of all kinds should
be eaten frequently Salads form ideal
spring luncheon dishes. and as differ
ent salad can be devised every day for
a month without much trouble, they
need never grow monotonous Fish
faxed and mixed with French dress
ing, minced green pepper and celery,
tomatoes garnished with celery. green
pepper, diced cucumber, crumbed eggs.
olives, radishes, nuts and green onions,
cold cooked cauliflower, asparagus.
spinach, carrots and string beans
dressed with French dressing and
served on lettuce. and cold peas, corn
cut from the cob. and other later vege-


tables with lettuce. and such other
greens as endive. kale. chicory and
water-cress are all delicious salads.
Fresh fruits should form the spring
dessert as often as possible. Gelatin
desserts, custards and water ice or ice
cream are other light desserts that are
far preferable to heavier puddings and
pastry that pass muster in the winter
time.

Rome. July 24.-The great battle for
Gorilla is still raging on the Isonzo front.
Austrian re-enforcements having arrived,
numerous counter-attacks have been de-
livered against the Italians, but all have
failed.


Gen. Cardona, in his latest report.
says the Italian forces are still shatter-
ing the Austrian columns. which are
being hurled against them At all points
they have been driven back with heavy
losses. The Austrian attacks on the
Italian left have been very severe.


The movement was one of the most
daring and costly counter offensives the
Austrians have made. Following the Ger
man tactics they advanced in dense
masses. seeking by sheer weight of num-
bers to overwhelm the Italians first
line. Although severely pressed. the Ital-
ians stood their ground bravely. At
the critical moment, Gen. Cardona was
able to throw fresh troops into the fl ut
and the reserves hurled themselves
against the Austrians with extraordinary
energy, relieving the pressure on the
first line.


Austrians Moved Down


The result of this maheuver was that
the new troops arrested the Austrian at
lacks and ultimately threw them back in
disorder. the Italians taking 800 pris-
oners. including seventy-six officers.


The Italian artillery. rendered SPLEEN
did service. When the Austrians show
ed themselves in mass formation. Gen
Cardona's guns simply moved them
down. Consequently. it was with A con-
siderably diminished force that they
rushed against the Italian wall of in
fantry.


Thus ended another phase of the pro-
longed and still continuing battle.

pictures.

city has just written home:


The Twenty-third London Regiment.
after faithfully and steadily doing trench
duty for about two months. was ordered
to charge. They did so coolly and effect
lively. They succeeded in taking three
lines Of trenches by brilliant dash, but
they were shelled out of two lines by
terrible enfilade Smelling, which caused
more casualties than the charge, many
men being blown to pieces.

under terrible machine gun and artillery
fire. In one instance forty-seven men
held a trench against overwhelming odds.
The Germans threw petrol bombs. Many
men were blinded and roamed about
without sight between the lines. The
whole was a terrible and unnerving sight

Little Serbia, who stood her ground so

Germany's great march to the sea, via
Constantinople. Germany and Bulgaria
have joined hands and may soon obtain
all the supplies they may need through
the Mediterranean Sea.


The English blockade would thus be-
come practically useless, which should
help to bring to an amicable settlement

States is having with that country.


Three thousand Serbs have been taken

ignored by the allies. Though England
has stated number of times that Ser
bia would have all the assistance needed,
the assistance was not Forthcoming, the
Anglo French army ID now embarking at
Salonika and, 1t il expected, will attack
the railroad through Serbia, Bulgaria
and Turkey, a distance Of $50 miles.
Though the forces of the allies will
seek to stop the Teutonic forces from
gaining the vantage ground of the Bos-
phorus, the Bulgarians are so disposed
that the Serbians are practically hem


med in; Turks are guarding the Bull
garian Black sea; and the points where
Russia is likely to attack are covered and
the ports are heavily mined.


It would seem that this is the most
important victory for the Teutons that
has been achieved. Let them beat the
combined forces now, and it gives them
access to the markets of the Mediter-
ranean.

Form triumphed when Boston beat
Philadelphia in the world series. The
American League team was stronger
all around than its opponent. Phila-
delphia won in the National League
by playing steadily throughout the sea-
son. while other teams were doing well
one week and going to pieces the next
week. With one star pitcher, two star
batters and one star fielder Philadelphia
had little difficulty in besting the weak
ened teams in the older circuit.

cutfielders, one phenomenal infielder,

difference in playing strength-posslbiy

The fact is that in the last four or five
years the American League has been
drawing away more and more from the
National League. The victory of the Bos-
ton Nationals last year was flash IN the
nan. Of the last five worlds series the
American League has captured four.
The clubs which gave the older organiza-
ton its prestige-the Giants. the Cubs,
the Pittsburgh Pirates-have become en-
feebled and demoraized. Old players
Lave been retained too long and dry rot
has set in.


On the other hand, the American
League has been developing new talent
end keeping the playing standard high.
As an instance, Shore, Foster and Leon
ard, Boston's pitchers, were unknown in
1912, when the Boston Americans de-
feated the Giants for the Worlds Cham
All Boston's pitchers in 1912,
except Wood, have disappeared. Yet the
Giants started out the season of 1915
on veterans of 1912 and prior
seasons. like Mathewson, Marquard and
Tesreau.


Boston beat Philadelphia four games
out of five. The Chicago Americans beat
the Chicago Nationals four games out Of
five. The St. Louis Americans beat the
St. Louis Nationals four games out Of
five. There are three other teams in the
American League besides Boston-De-
troit, Chicago and Washington-which
probably could have defeated Philadel-
phia. The lesson Of the series to the
National League is therefore unmistak-
able. Reorganization, new blood on the
diamond and a sharper standard Of play
are required to bring it up even again
with its younger, more progressive rival.

Columbia, Mo, Oct 4.-Mrs. Annie
Fisher couldn't consistently get
cross if some one did tell her that
her beaten biscuit were like bricks,
because she lives in a house built
with them. Moreover, she collects
the rent from fourteen others also
built with them.


Mrs. Fishers biscuit always just
naturally melted in the mouth. No
one in Columbia ever has been able
to describe them, any more than
rainbow or a bird-song or any other
natural wonder can be described.
The only outlet for the emotion which
the eating of one of Mrs. Fishers
biscuits evoked was telling the next
person one met: You certainly
ought to taste those biscuits"


And, of course, that was how it
all started, this buiscuit business that
bought SO ,muehxreal estate and solid
independence


One person told about them, and
another fellow did likewise; and so
Mrs. Fishers fame grew and grew,
and flowed over the state line, and
trickled into the four corners of the
states, and finally went meandering
across the ocean.


AS the receipts from grateful din
ers kept coming in, Mrs. Fisher
turned them all into real estate, and
stayed right on the job, only rolling
down her sleeves long enough to
have her picture taken the other
morning. Another odd thing about
Mrs. Fisher is that she doesn't raise
her prices ION account of the war" or
the high cost of living, or even for
the commonest reason of all-suc-
cess. Those biscuits of hers started
their career at 121s cents per dozen,
and at 12h cents they have stayed
| While her biscuits are her main
stay, on the side Mrs Fisher makes
fruit cake and wedding cake and
other symbolic and dangerous concoc-
tions, and also on the side she car
ries on quite a large catering busi
ness.


This pleasant home of Mrs. Fishers
has fourteen rooms, and is equipped
with all the modern conveniences.


OF course, colored women are the
traditional best cooks" and it isn't
strange that numbers of them have
very successfully entered the cater
ing business. Another profession for
which ther race traditionally fits
them is that of nursing; but, so far
at least, ambitious young colored
nurses have had a hard row to hoe

ed. Martin sprinted. too, and the

of cubic yards of dirt into the Panama Canal and
upset plans for the official ceremonies to celebrate

President will be there. Prof Taft and Col Roose-

battleship to convey him to the scene.

signs that the chasm between New Haven and
Oyster Bay is narrowing. If Col Goethals can
subdue Culebra Cut before the Fourth-wel, who

pine and crowsfoot are to be found in
masses under the dead leaves by road

ty. which blooms all winter where

fascinating candle shades and gar

ming leaves over candle shades and

Boston, Aug 15.-Many policemen
we're injured to-day when 1900 Ital-
ian reservists, who were to sail on the
steamer Canopic tonight, made riot
Gus demonstrations against the in
termed German steamships Amerika
and Cincinnati. Sailors on the Ger
man vessels were struck by flying
stones and sticks and revolver shots
were exchanged between the police
and the reservists and their friends.


In an earlier disturbance which de-
yeloped during the forming of a
parade of the Italians in North Square,
three police officers were injured, one
being stabbed. Ten arrests were made
in both outbreaks.


The body of reservists, said to be
the largest to leave this country on
one ship since the war began, in
Guided Italians from all over New
England. They paraded in two sec
tons to the Commonwealth Pier. in
the South Boston district. On one
side lay the Canop.c. On the other
the Amerika and the Cincinnati, Of
the Hamburg Line, have
been interned since the war began.


Police Rescue Three Germans.


Most of the reservists made their
way aboard the Canopic, while the
crowd which accompanied them moved
about the pier. When two stewards
from the Cincinnati, in their uniforms,
appeared on the pier, the crowd first
booed, and then iostled them. Both
resisted and were Joined by a watch
man. The three men were beaten
badly before they were rescued by
the police.


The crowd angered by the rescue,
began to lombard the big German
liners with stones, smashing portfolio
glasses and deck fittings. Sailors on
the decks also became targets and sew
eral were struck.


During this disturbance Patrolman
Frederick A. Peterson, in attempting to
arrest a man, was attacked from be-
hind and beaten down with a stone
Drawing his revolver he took his man
in custody and. with the assistance of
other officers, locked him up in a room
on the pier.


L. S. Customs Station Stoned.


The mob formed again, and after
being harangued by several speakers
rushed to the main pier building. The
United States customs station was
stoned, but eight officers forced the
crowd back at the point of revolvers.
Shots were fired in the air and were
answered from the crowd.


Numerous policemen required hos
pital attention after this melee, head
injuries, broken leg, wrenched arms
and severe contusions being among
their complaints.


The North Square riots, according to
the police, developed from the attempt
OF some of the reservists to make fell
low countrymen who were not going to
sail with them shout their allegiance
to the old flag. Officers attempted to
quell these small disturbances, only to
have both sides turn upon them. and
stones were thrown and knives shown
ty the crowd. One officer was slashed
across the cheek and arms.

proached the feeling became more tense
Mexicans began making preparations

Columbus Day (Oct. 12) has come and
gone and the city has kept on its tread
mill way, punctuating its tedium with
few more automobile accidents and the
various smaller happenings which come
with the rising tide of noon and sweep
back again with the receding hours OF
the night.


Few in this great city have thought of
the man who revolutionized the science
of astronomy and. by his marvellous
mind and invincible courage, brought to
view a vast new continent.


There is little in the whole history of
the world to compare with the act of this
solitary individual who, against all OPP
position derision. scorn, poverty and the
wisdom of the times, kept his soul free
and swerved not from his purpose until it
was accomplished.


To Isabella of CASTLE, the advanced
woman of her day, who was able to see
his vision and willing to part with her
Jewels, the only thing she possessed, in
order that it might be realized, we owe
allegiance and debt we can only repay
by helping others who may come with
new inspiration for the future.


There is probably no proposition which
COuIu &c put oCiutC TIC puouS toudy eitdt
would in any way approach the magni-
tude and audacity which this idea held
for the Europe Of the 18th century.


From our own manner of receiving
anything which deviates from our well
trodden paths of thought: our suspicious
of the sanity of the perpetrator of the
new thought; our secret intolerance, the
impossibiliy Of inducing the public to
lend sympathetic ear, we may have
some slight conception of the difficulties
which confronted Columbus in his under
taking. Madness. suicide, everything
Enthusiastically. was the general verdict.


When he had finally gotten his three
little ships and had sailed for weeks.
straining his eyes for sight of the land
he could not see, his sailors rebelled and
turned the prows toward home.


Still his faith was unweakened and he
plead with them for just three days
more, and that faith which can move
mountains, found response in the hearts
of the men, for they sullenly agreed.


Three days, which he probably spent in
the PROV of his vessel. looking ahead into
the vast unknown. and then despair must
have settled upon him: when on the
ocean, rising and falling upon the waves
foated branch with fresh, green leaves.


In few hours there arose from the
sea a cloud-ike island in the distance.
Then did he fall on his knees and thank
God, and joy (which passeth under
standing" must have welled up through
his entire being.

Austro-Hungarian Headquarters, Aug.

taken mainly with the bayonet, reports
received here declare. The Croatian
and Cracow infantry are said to have
distinguished themselves in charges
against the southern and western
fronts, while the German reserve corps
forced its way into the citadel and
town from the north.


The Russians had erected a new line
of works beyond the swamps encircling
the fortress, three to four kilometres
outside the permanent fort girdle, had
fortified it strongly and provided il
with ten series of barbed wire en-
tanglements and broad field of buried
mines.


The storming began late in the after
noon of August 25. The infantry of
Field Marshal Won ARR advanced on
both sides of the Viala turnpike. They
hewed their way with intrenching tools
and gun butts through the entange
ments under heavy rifle and machine
gun fire and charged the forts with the
bayonet.


The cheering infantry in the gather
ing darkness charged fort after fort,
advancing recklessly over hidden mine
fields and springing into the works.
They engaged in a desperate hand-to-
hand struggle with the stubbornly re-
sisting Russians. The last fort was
taken by II o'clock at night.


The Russian survivors across the
Bug River were destroying the bridges
behind them The Austro- Uungsrian
forces pursued them vigorously, and
reached the river at o'clock in the
morning, where they were obliged to
await the arrival of pontoons. The
Germans, in the mean time attacking
from the north, carried this sector Of
the fort girdle, and, unhampered by
the river, stOrmed the citadel and
forced a way into the town.


The Russians fred the city in their
retreat. Most of the $4,000 inhabitants
evacuated before the siege, and only a
few remain. The amount of spoils
taken has not yet been ascertained.

London, March % Frank Moran. the

OF Hull. the -Persimmop. -nf Grimsby,

At the opening of the great German
offensive against Russia the armies OF the
Car in Galicia were in the Carpathlans,
their flank toward Germany protected by
strong defensive works behind the Dun
ajec-Biala rivers.


The first operation was directed against
this flank. which was suddenly struck by a
huge army under Mackensen provided
with an enormous artillery train. In few
DAYS the entire front crumpled up, uncov-
erinp the rear of the armies in the Car
pafhians. Along the Dunajec the Rus
slams suffered real disaster, losing thou
sands IN prisoners. In the first stages OF
their retreat more thousands were capt
ured and the whole Carpathian army was
threatened in front by the Austrian armies
coming from Hungary, in flank and rear
by the German troops coming east IN
Galicia.


Efforts to stand at the Wislok the San
and at the Grodek lakes failed. Although
the Russian resistance steadily stitfened,
the German advance could not be checked.
Jaroslav, Przemysl and finally Lemberg
were recaptured and the Russians were
driven north into Poland and east toward
the Bessarabian frontier. All but thin
strip of Galicia was reconquered, after
having been occupied by Russia since Sep
TENDER.


Russian disaster was explained by the
lack of ammunition and by the great supe-
riority of German artillery. Probably this
explains the rapidity of the debacle, but
the Russians were clearly outnumbered,
outgeneraled and outfought.

distinctly solemn aspect. No horns were

lively few men were present. Former

nothing to co.

where usually merry crowds welcomed

amusement was omitted. That the

Bile. All the amusement places in Ber-

Miss Claire Galligan, of New Rochelle.

Beach. who finished second. Both used

Miss Helen Rubican, rne little thir-

atfording absolutely equal and fair

1t was a stirring fight between these
two for half mile, but Miss Galligan''
cleaner, smoother stroke carried her t

/ of nearly fifteen yards. Miss Rubicar
swung around fifty yards behind Mis-
Freeman. The Misses Pearlstein, Fret
tag and Greenfield came along next

On the second leg the margin be
/ tween the leaders increased steadily

1 ing fourth place. Miss Hyatt withdrew

Thus the field reached the last turn
and headed for home, Miss Freeman
making a game and desperate attempt
to catch her speeding rival in the
stretch. But the latter quickened her
pace in prompt response and, swim
ming in perfect form, reached the line
an easy winner


Miss Freeman gave n pretty exhibit
tion OF craftsmanship on finishing.
Swiftly climbing onto the float, she

SYDNEY Australia, November 25.-
The trial of strength between the New
South Wales Base Ball Association and
the National Base Ball League of New
South Wales has ended in half and
half victory for each organization. The
association had controlled base ball in
New South Wales and had confined its
activities to games in the winter. The
league depended upon the popularity of
summer base ball, and had gradually
become the rival of the association.
A few weeks ago the association found
itself forced to try to provide summer
games for it's members. many Of whom
were cricketers as well as base ball
players


The opening of the summer base ball
season today found the association
without a team. The league has
twenty-four clubs. This proved ap..
parently that among the members or
the association there was not the de-
mand for summer base ball that many
followers of the American sport had
expected and that cricketers would pre-
fer to play the old game. The associa-
ton has now decided to drop the idea
Of summer games altogether.

Furnes, Belgium, Aug. 17.-The
famous bridgehead at Dixmude, thrice
lost and thrice retaken by the Bel
gians, remained in their hands this
morning after desperate assault by
the Germans had been lepulsed.


The bridgehead is fragment of the
right bank of the User beyond the Dix
nude bridge. The Germans hold all
the adjoining ground, but the Bel
gians have chung to the position av-
preached by the bridge since October,
warding off incessant German attacks
and enduring daily Smelling. The
Germans, attracted by the exposed Bel
gian position, frequently have attacked
in mass formation, and it is estimated
they lost 5000 men there from October
to August 1.


After three attempts the Germans
had abandoned direct efforts to occupy
the trenches, but kept up fire from
three sides. Every evening at the kour
of relief German field guns and Cat
lings played on the position and the
communicating trenches. Every even
ing a few Belgians fell. The position
was useless in the absence Of gen
eral attack, but it had cost so much
the Belgians held on. Machine guns
were posted on the left bank, with
several batteries of three-inches be-
hind them.


No relief was sent last evening, bu:
the occupying detachment evacuated
the trenches under the protection OF
artillery and machine guns. Then the
gunners waited for the attack, which
came in the early morning. The Gel-
mans were permitted to advance four
deep without molestation until they
came within range of the machine guns,
which opened fire supported by the
three-inches. Most of the attacking
force fell before they reached the
trench of the bridgehead, and the Bel
eian guns had the range so well that
those who got into the trenches were
obliged to abandon them.

! BY EVELYN L. HAYNES (aged 40.
High in white, heecy drifts the snow


was piled, and sparkling with bright,
frosty crystals were the bare trees one


morning when Jack and Jill looked out
through the one bare spot on the win


dow that was not covered with frost


and saw the wonders nature had


wrought during the night.


With anxious haste they dressed.


After breakfast they hurried out into


the white world. SO deep was the snow


that they ploughed Though it with


difficulty, but at last they succeeded in


reaching the back yard. Here, they de-
cided, was the ideal spot for a snow
hut, and they were right.


By noon they had built a large hui,
into which several children could crawl.
Inside the hut they put an old rug and
few boxes, on which to sit. During
the afternoon a crowd of children
helped Jack and Jill make slide,
winch reached the length Of the yard,
and there they played till dark and
supper was ready.


The next day was Sunday, and they
did not play in the snow hut. but on
Monday after school all the children
gathered in the yard for a SNOWFALL
fight. And such a fight! The chill
dren's mother finally had 10 stop IT,,
because many Of them were hit and
nearly beaded as one little girl with
SNOWFALL down her neck expressed il,
Then came supper and bed, into which
Jack and Jill tumbled. tired but happy.


Several days later. as a guard 20 the
hut, Jack made a snow man. and Jill
put on the finishing touches. When
the first newness Of the snow had worn
off and the hut was becoming forgot
ten, Jack and Jill went up the hill to
coast with fun and laughter. But Jack
did not fall down and break his crown,
neither did Jill come tumbling after.
Both were good children, and Jack was
very careful TO see that Jill was kept
safe from such dangers as being hit by
a hard SNOWFALL or pushed into a snow
bank by some big bully.


However. as we all know. winter fun
soon begins to grow tiresome, and little
folks long for spring, when the grass
grows green and the soft breexes whis-
per through the trees and The birds
begin 10 sing and everything awakes.


So let US leave the two children still
playing in the Ssow hut and coasting
downhill, but waiting with certain
happy feeling that spring will soon be
here.

Won Bernstorff the German Ambassador,
and DR.. Constantin Theodor Dumba, Am
bassador from Austria-Hungary, whose
recall has been demanded by the United
States, held a secret conference this
afternoon.

remained hidden in his hotel. but shortly
after 1870 o'clock. Count Won Bernstorff

ground passage connecting the hostelry

Austrian Embassy, was the man who
carried the Dumba summons to Won
Bernstorff. Within a few minutes after
he reached Won Bernstorff's hotel the two
jumped into a taxicab and were whirled
away.

ried in pursuit, reaching the hotel at
the same time as the Teuton diplomats.

next door. None was allowed to follow

saw a little peasant girl dying from the
bayonet wounds in her back which the Ger
man soldiers had given her.
Cain slew only brother,


lad who was fair and strong,
His murder was careless and honest,


A heated and sudden wrong.
And Judas was kindly and pleasant,


For he shared an invincble man
But you--you have spitted the children,
As they toddled and stumbled and ran.
She heard you sing on the high-road,


She thought you were gallant and gay;
Such men as the peasants Of Flanders:
The friends of child at play.
She saw the sun on your helmets,


The sparkle Of glancing light
She saw your bayonets flashing,


And she laughed at your Prussisn might
Then you gave her death for her laughter
As you looked on her mischevous face.
You hated the tiny peasant,


With the hate Of your famous race.
You were not frenzied and angry;


You were cold and efficient and keen.
Your thrust was AS thorough and deadly
As the stroke OF faithful machine.
You stabbed her deep with your rife:


You had good reason to sing,
As YOU footed it on through Flanders


Past the broken and quivering thing.
Something impedes your advancing,


A dragging has come on your hosts.
And Paris grows dim now, and DINNER,
Through the blur Of your raucous boasts
Your singing IL sometimes broken


By cultural German groans.
Your ankles are wet with her bleeding,
Your pike is blunt from her bones.
The little peasant has tripped you.


She hangs 20 your bloody stride.
And the dimpled hands are fastened


Where they fumbed before she died.

London, March 25.-"The Admiralty
has good reason to believe that the
German submarine U-29 has been sunk,
with all hands, This news was pub
lished in the foregoing official form
late this evening. The Admiralty gave
no details of how or where the U-29
was sunk, but the report that she was
disposed of was received in shipping
circles with a sigh of relief.


1t was this vessel which, just fort
night ago, torpedoed six steamers in
the Bristol Channel and off the Scilly
Islands within two days. Her COM
mander, who spoke English perfectly
and who treated the crews of the tor
pedoed vessels with great considera-
tion, told one of the merchant cap
tains who was taken aboard the sub
marine, that he was the commander Of
the submarine which torpedoed the
British cruisers Aboukir, Cressy and
Hogue. If this was true, he was the
man looked upon as Germany's most
daring submarine navigator.


This makes the sixth German sub
marine that the British Admiralty has
reported sunk, five of them at least by
British warships. In only one case so
far has the British report been denied
by the Germans. Besides these, a
French warship recently sank a sub
marine off the French coast. and three
British merchant captains have put in
claims for the rewards offered for mer-
chantmen ramming German underwater
craft. One of these claims, that of the
captain OF the steamer ThOrdis, has
been allowed by the Admiralty and the
reward paid.


The Dutch steamer Medea was sunk
Oft Beachy Head this morning by the
German submarine U-2S. She carried
cargo of oranges, and was bound
from Salonica for London.


The Medea was stopped by the sub
marine and the crew were given fifteen
minutes in which 70 leave the vessel.
They did so. and the submarine then
fired several shots at the steamer,
which remained afoat for an hour. The
crew rowed about in their boats until
picked up by destroyer, which
brought them to Dover. The Admiralty,
in reporting the sinking of the Medea,
says:


THE ship was flying the Dutch flag
and had a Dutch crew aboard. Her
name, Medea, Amsterdam was painted
in large letters on her sides The
ships papers were taken by the Ger
mans. who refused 10 return them"

tackled By a submarine to-day. A tor
pedo passed within ten feet of the
fishing boat while she was crossing the
Channel. A British patrol boat chased
the submarine, which, however, disap-
neared

or German.

menian patriarch, who argued that he
could not communicate with the priests
IN the provinces in any of the permitted
languages and thus fulfill his religious
mission. Then protested the Greeks, who
number millions in the Turkish empire.
Bulgaria pointed out that this was not
fair treatment for a friendly govern
ment. She was followed by the Italian
and American ambassadors.


The Turkish government seemed to rec
ognize the fairness of these representa-
tons, for a new communique was issued.
reading as follows:


Apart from the already mentioned Ian
Euages, the postoffice is allowed to carry
correspondence written in Armenian.
Greek, Bulgarian, Italian. and AmeH-
can languages"


Thus the American language" is for

The steamboat Tennessee, Of the Bay
State Line, participant in one Of
those inexplicable accidents Of the sea.
came to her berth yesterday az Pier 10,

structure on the port side. where the
bow Of a three-masted schooner, the
Samuel 8. Thorp, ploughed into her at
1880 p. m. on Saturday in Long Island
Sound, off Watch Hill.


One passenger, seriously injured IN
the back, lies in the French Hospital,
in Thirty-fourth Street, and five others
who had minor bruises went to their
homes in this city when they landed
from the Colonial Line steamboat Con-
cord, which took them aboard In mid
Sound soon after the collision.


officers of the Tennessee, as well as
the frightened travellers, who were
reused from sleep by the intrusion of
the schooner, were puzzled yesterday
over two things-the miracle of escape
from death and serious injury of all
on board and the cause of such col
lision. The night was clear. and the
steamboat, heavily laden with freight





staterooms, left Providence stimuli
taneously with the steamboat Concord.


Robert j. Noble, general manager Of
the Bay State Line, says the Concord
and Tennessee were abeam off Fisher
Island when the schooner was first
sighted Her course lay between the
two passenger carriers, and it was as
sume6 that she would take care Of
herself and come through. The sailing
lights were plainly visible on the three
vessels. The schooner vas running
free before a northwest wind, but sud
denly she bore over to the Tennessee.
The big bowsprit plunged into the
steamer near the wheelhouse and
ripped up seven staterooms that shell
tered about fifteen sleeping passengers.
Two more rooms were shattered before
the big stick broke off and, dangling
from its headgear, went on with the
schooner.


Everybody was reused by the crash
and the heeling over of the Tennessee.
Captain George B. Enos, master OF the
damaged boat, soon saw that she was
seaworthy, and instructed his officers to
calm the frightened passengers, whose
shrieks gave rise 70 the bellet tnat
many had been seriously injured.


A call for help was promptly sent out
by wireless and several vessels re-
sponded. The Concord, less than half
mile away, came over and made fast 70
the Tennessee. Although the pas
senrers could have remained aboard
the damaged vessel with safety, Cap
tain Enos thought II wiser to transfer
them TO the Concord. The steamboats,
were lashed together. and the TRANSFER
was made within half an hour.


The schooner was picked up by the
rug Mohican and towed TO New London
for repairs. She was bound from Perth
Amboy for Newburyport, Mass. The
Concord landed the Tennessee's pas
sengers IN this city at $3.50 a. m. yes
terday, and the injured vessel came IN
later. landing the baggage. The dam
age to the Tennessee is estimated at
about $4,000.


The crash recalls a sidewiping that
occurred of the Brazilian coast many
wears ago in broad daylight, when a
Steamship out Of Southampton, bound
for Rio dc Janeiro, hit another vessel
Of the came line, northbound from
Buenos Ayres. Both had tho bread At
lantic TO manpuvre in; both had OBJ
served each other coming for half an
hour; nevertheless they scraped SIDES
and passed on TO their respective des-
tinations.

gian professor, who buried his entire
fortune, consisting of $4,000 worth
of stocks. bonds. jewels, gold and
plate. in his garden at Malines. before
he fed from that city, has just re-
ceived word from the United States
consul at Malines that his property is
safe and has been taken under the
guardianship of the United States gov
eminent. The house was bombarded
and later burned to the ground, but
the buried treasure in the garden was
not disturbed.


Some time after he reached London
the professor went to the American
embassy here, gave them detailed plan
of his house and garden and told them
Where his treasure was hid. The
search was successfully carried out by
the American consul at Malines and
the property is now registered in his
name, pending its release from Ger
man trusteeship, when the war is over.

Wichita Falls, Tex. Nov. 1s~-All six
of the machines of the United States
Military Aeroplane Squadron from
Fort Sill reached here safely to-day,
making the fight in less than an hour.


The flight was made under almost
perfect weather conditions. The pilots
experienced no trouble with their ma
chimes, and two minutes covered the
difference between the slowest and
fastest time. Lieutenant J. E. Carberry,
the first 1ier to land, took thirty-nine
minutes to cover the forty-five miles.
The machines took ali elevation of 5000
feet


The aviators will continue their fight
tomorrow, when they will set out for
Fort Worth, ia miles away. From
there they will fly 70 the government
Headquarters at Fort Sam Houston,
where the fight will end on Wednes-
day, unless accidents interfere.


The fight is the first of its kind at
tempted by army aviators, and will be
made throughout under conditions as
nearly like those encountered in war
time as possible. The squadron Is com
posed of fifteen aviators and ninety
men. Those who do not fly accompany
a motor repairing equipment, which
precedes the aviators and prepares suit
able landing places for them.

London, June S.--One Belgian, three
Norwegian and one British vessel-fve
in all form the toll taken in one day
by German submarines. In one case a
woman and young girl were among
the drowned. In another case, after
giving the crew ten minutes to quit
the threatened steamer, the submarine
towed the Loats for thirty minutes
until trawler hove in sight.


The most notable case was that of
the Belgian steamer Menapier, sent to
the bottom by torpedo off the North
Foreland, opposite the mouth of the
Thames. Out of twenty-three persons
on board only six were saved. The cap
tain, his wife and his daughter. the
first mate and the pilot and twelve
members of the crew lost their lives.


The Norwegian victims are the
Trudvang. Superb and Glittertind.
The Trudvang was hailed by a Ger
man submarine soon after mid day
yesterday when off St. Anne's Head
The captain was ordered to bring his
papers aboard the submarine, whose
commander gave the crew twenty
minutes TO take to the boats.


The submarine then sent twelve
shells into the Trudvang. The shoot
ing brought out patrol boat from
Milford Haven, which picked up the
skipper and crew, numbering thirteen,
from the boats. During the operation
the submarine attempted vainly to tor
pedo the patrol boat The men from
the Trudvang were landed to-day at
Milford Haven.


Ten Minutes Leeway.


The crew of the Glittertind was
landed to-day in the Tyne. The yes
sci, with a cargo of lumber. was on
her way from Sweden to Hartlepool
when she encountered a German sub
marine. The Germans gave the crew
ten minutes to take to the boats be-
fore firing a torpedo.


The submarine towed the ships
boats for thirty minutes until trawl-
er hove in sight.


The Glittertind was Of 376 tons net.
built in 1918. She was ls6 feet long.


The Trudvang was a steamer Of $40
tons net register, built at Bergen in
1897. She was 224 feet long, 81 feet
beam and l3 feet deep.


The Superb was a bark Of ,293 tons,
built at Glasgow in 1875. She sailed
from Buenos Ayres March 10 for
Queenstown.

All the events we're run off fiawless-

Austrian aviators made an unsuccessful

wildly.

warning from the guards that they should
enter the cellar of the residence.

the Priucesses. After dropping all their

The Cadillac Eight has shattered an
other record-this time racing with a
Union Pacific special train from Denver
to Cheyenne. and arriving at the station
two minutes before the train.


The regular schedule of the Union
Pacific between Denver and Cheyenne is
three hours; but Engineer Charles Burg
dorf. of the Denver Post Special. which
carried 100 of Denvers most prominent
business men to Cheyenne for the From
tier Day celebration. was instructed
to make the run in two hours and fiji
teen minutes. Burgdorf was true to his
trust. but when he pulled his train into
the Cheyenne station after his record
run he found that the Cadillac Eight
had preceded him by two minutes.


All Union Pacific records for the run.
however, were broken; and the special
at one time touched n speed of eighty
miles an hour. which is said to be the
fastest locomotive has ever travelled
in Colorado.


Much interest was evidenced in the
race, and the towns along the route
covered by the motor cars permitted the
racers to pass through at top speed.
Work was suspended in most places
along the route where throngs turned
out to watch the contest. At times the
road parallels the railroad tracks. which
made the race the more exciting espe-
cially when the locomotive and the Cadil-
lie fought for the lead.


The motor cars were forced to travel
ZIG miles. while the trains mileage was
112. Its smooth tracks gave the train
another great advantage, for part of the
distance covered by the motor cars there
was practically no road at all.


Despite these handicaps. Harold Brink
err averaged better than fifty miles an
hour with his Cadillac Eight and reached
the goal two minutes ahead of the fast
flying special.


Engineer Burgdorf had the satisfac-
ton, however. OF beating the other ten
motor cars entered, as the second one
to finish is said to have been thirty min
utes behind the Cadillac.

Beautifully simple, wasn't il? And

tidious appetite:


Baker With Cheese.


Drain boiled asparagus and arrange
the stalks neatly on buttered baking
dish. Fry a chopped onion in butter
and pour this over the asparagus.
Sprinkle over it bread crumbs and
grated cheese and bake brown. The
asparagus can be cut into one-inch

Fried Asparagus.


Boil the asparagus, drain it. dip each
fry in deep fat. Serve with cream

Dreamed.


Cut a bunch or two of asparagus

tender. Drain and put into rich, white
sauce. rather thick. for the aspara-

rika, and serve very hot.


In Rolls.


Remove the center from stale. rather
long, pointed rolls and fry the rolls

brown paper and keep hot. Cut a
bunch of asparagus, in the meantime,
into one-inch lengths and boil until
tender. Drain and put in i double
boiler with cup of milk. Add the
yolhs of five eggs and stir until thick

little grated nutmeg. and pour into the

instead Of the egg sauce if desired.

tered baking dish. Season with salt
and pepper, dot with bits of butter,
sprinkled with curmbs and finely
minced boiled eggs. Add more aspara-
until the dish is filed. Have crumbs
on top and bake brown.


Served Cold.


Boil until tender stalks of asparagus

them with mayonnaise, with Holland
aise or with tartare sauce. 1t can also
be served with a sauce of oil and vine
gar. sprinkled with chopped cucumber

Boiled.

text:
Even after war had been declared and
the troops we're actually on the march.
Barbara Heathcote failed 70 realize the
gravity Of the situation. Comfortably
ensconced in her great country bunga-
low. surrounded by servants and every
luxury, she did not see the necessity Of
worrying about war which would not
upset her own weil-ordered existence


Barbara had not stopped to realize that
the little village in Bedfordshire was
right on the line Of march. nor did she
know that being householder. she
would be ordered to provide temporary
shelter for officers and men OF the troops
when they should pass on the way to
backgrounds.


II was with great surprise that she
found herself watching an OFFICER re-
treating from her door having bileted
a score OF soldiers on her. She had been
asked lin the name OF the king" to
provide shelter for a day or two for the
men on the march. and Barbara had
been first indignant, then Indifferent. Her
servants, she decided. could make pro-
vision for the soldiers


But Barbaras equilibrium was upset.
War had been forced into her conscious
ness and she wished the troops had taken
another route to the backgrounds. She
disliked annoyance of any kind, for she
was selfish and self-centred.


Where will these troops sleep?" she
asked of her old servant.


ION the veranda, Miss Barbara, and
In the garden" replied Jenkins, more ex-
cited than the soldiers themselves. I'VE
will feed them In the servants hall"


When Jenkins had gone Barbara's brow
puckered. She well knew that fighting
men were accustomed to hardship, but
the thought of them sleeping on wooden
floors or perhaps in the dew-dampened
garden was not pleasant. Certainly 1t
would disturb her owns night rest to
have them there. During the day, how
ever, she tried to harden herself by the
thought that there was much worse ahead
of them than sleeping in sheltered gar
dens.


In the evening, when a score or more
OF tired but laughing soldiers in khaki
came trooping through the great hedge
gate Barbara watched them with quickly
beating heart. Somehow and without
warning a sharp emotion fripped her. She
tried to stife a desire to cry and won
dering why she should feel so helpless all
Of sudden. The men were big and
brave and were going off happily to fight
for their country and their womenfolk
She, Barbara, who was nourished and
cared for as II she were a hothouse bud,
was miserable, and the realization of her
own smallness dawned on her.


She looked again at the men, now
going toward the back of the house, and
their war kits brought fresh emotion to
Barbaras heart. They were going to
battle for perhaps months, and maybe
years, with that small provision for COM
fort. Never before had Barbara seen
the troops in full war kit, and the mea-
gerness of their equipment appalled, her
She who had slept beneath rose-colored
eiderdowns all her life could conceive
OF nothing so terrible as that pitiful sup
ply of human comforts. She turned from
the window and to the telephone.


Jenkins she called down to her old
servant, "see that cook provides the best
of everything for these men. Spare no
expense or trouble to make them COM
Portable"


When she had hung up the receiver
Barbara felt trihe more like herself.
After all, most OF the men would return
from the war. She was upsetting her
self for vague fears. She tried to throw
of the chastity pictures that the sight
of the troops had put before her, but It
was useless, now that her very doorstep
was thronged with soldiers to feel other
than fearful for their fate. Again she
wished that the burden of worry had
not been flung upon her. The thought
sent a wave of shame over her. Perhaps
for the first time in her entire life Bar
bara knew how despicably selfish she
was She was regretting the entrance
into her life Of that score of brave men.

Sir: In a letter to you Mr.. Slashk as

Among the many evil characters Of the

foremost In the words "our own land"
both of these bad characteristics are sui
fcently picturized | am very anxious 10
know from whence Serbia has any right to
these portions of lands.


Bosnia Herzegovina were originally under
the Turkish rule. At the Congress Of Berlin
in 1873 the powers conceded TO Austria the
right TO occupy those Turkish provinces.
Austria then invaded Bosnia. But the in
habitants resisted, and only after a long and
hard fight could Austria gain control OF the
territory. But the bloodshed was not ended.
In the wild and rugged mountains there lived
reckless, turbulent tribes which refused 70

safe They raided the villages, carrying OF

some elements. Thousands Of lives were
sacrificed in the preservation of law and or
der. Roads, railways and mines that were
built by the government were demolished by
the Bosnian mountaineers, and only sys-
tematic prosecution could gain the upper
hand. Tireless work made Bosnia Here
md inf fial %


After forty years Of unceasng labor the
loss of thousands of precious lives. the in
vestment of millions, Austria claimed the
territories for herself and annexed them as
crown lands. This was contrary to Serbia's
high flying plans. She hoped that after Aus
tria completed the work Of civilization she
would be presented with the cultured regions,
and thereby make the first step to be world
power. But when she began 10 realize that
Bosnia was lost forever her abominable
statesmen started the most despicable an
archistc campaign in history. And when, in
1908, Austria announced the permanent occu-
patton of the two Balkan provinces, Serbia's
indignation reached its top marx.


Serbia's agents swarmed through Austria.
They spread dissatisfaction among the up 20
then contented population; they whispered
irto the ears of the peasants false stories
about oppression and tyranny; preached a
questionable liberty 10 ignorant people and
corrupted the young generations with revo-
lutionary aspirations. From Belgrade came
plans of revolutions for the overthrow Of the
Hapsburg dynasty and the reduction of the
Dual Monarchy. The first open blow struck
az Austria was the assassination Of the Arch
duke Francis Ferdinand and his wife. But
Austria decided that it was also to be the last
blow. and after Serbia's unsatisfactory
answer TO her ultimatum she declared war.
! Never was there a more just war fought
than that of Austria against Serbia After
Serbia's hackers are defeated then her turn
will come and she will be eradiceted from the
list of the nations as punishment for her dis
graceful conduct.


Bosnia and Herzegovina belong 20 Austria,
as the Canal Zone belongs to the United
States. While the United States spent only
money on the zone the Dual Monarchy gave
both wealth and life for her Balkan posses
sons, and thereby gained an unquestionsble
right TO them. FRITZ ROSENTHAL.

The winning Of three lawn tennis
championships within twenty,1our
hours was the record completed by
Miss Molla Bjurstedt, the Norwegian
phenomenon of the courts, yesterday
afternoon, when she defeated MRS;
Marshall Mclean in the postponed
final round match of the Pelham Coun-
try Clubs annual invitation tourna-
ment. -,


Miss Bjurstedt won from Mrs. Nc

title of the Middle States at Mountain
Station, n. j., and the doubles title,

two hours. Mr.. and Mrs. B. +. Briggs,

busy with towels, mops, brooms and

In defeating Mrs Mclean yesterday

to the fact that there is no woman
PLAYER on the courts in this country
at present who can hope TO cope with
her. Mrs. Mclean, in the three times
she has encountered the Norwegian

champion her hardest matches, but
Yesterday she was beaten more easily

sions, and this in spite of the fact
that Miss Bjurstedt has been playing
on turf for the last month.

but Mrs. Mclean drew first blood by

could not at first control her wicked
forehand strokes, the change from turf
to clay apparently throwing her of
temporarily.


After Mrs. Mclean had gained lead
in games, however, the marvellous Nor
wegian girl began to reel off remark
ably well placed shots down the side
lines, which cut sharply across deep
court and forced Mrs. Mclean TO cover
a great amount of ground.


Several of the rallies between the
two were so fast that the gallery voiced
its appreciation generously. Mrs. Nc
Lean was fighting hard for the points
and carried four of the games 10 deuce
several times before Hiss BJurstedts
superior speed and harder hitting pre-

II was the ability Of the Morse star
TO force the issue at all stages that
won her the first set at 6-3. She was
always looking for the openings IN
Mrs. McLean's court, and once she dis
covered them she showed no hesitancy
in shooting the ball straight into the
unprotected territory.


Mrs. McLean's tactics were almost
purely defensive and so long as the
other made errors, the American girl
was safe. But Miss Bjurstedt was
too deadly in her placement shots and
at the net for such tactics to meet with
success.


Miss Biurstedt had won the first
game of the second set when the rain
came and everybody made rush for
the clubhouse veranda. Mrs. Nc
Lean started service when the match
was again taken up, and as before was
the quicker TO get going, winning her
own service and then breaking through
on her opponents.


Miss Biurstedt then began victori-
Gus sweep, however, her forehand

for brilliant session of net play -pon

More than once Mrs. McLean's drives
for deep court were taken on the full
volley from close TO the net by the
national champion, who placed them
with perfect judgment into the cor
ners, throwing Mrs. Mclean hopelessly
out of position. The Norwegian. ran
three games In row. bringing the
score TO 40, before Mrs. Mclean, by

her last game of the match.


Miss Bjurstedt raised the speei OF

east to the Atlantic seaboard weather
conditions are unprecedented. New
York, Pennsylvania and Ohio, with ad-
jacent territory, are in the grip of a
killing frost and grapes, peaches, cher
ries, plums and truck farms have been
hard hit.

and parts of Wyoming have expert
enced the most serious storms for

has kept steadily falling, crowding
rivers banks and levees.

from scattered sections and the in
jured will make long list. Several
cyclones have been reported.

January ).

Washington. Sept 3O.-Navy Depart
ment officials were enthusiastic today
over the experiments resulting for the
first time in transcontinental wireless
telephone communication.


By this means the human voice was
successfully transmitted yesterday
from the Arlington wireless plant to
the Mare Island, Cal, naval station, a
distance of $500 miles.


This achievement, together with the
successful operation of a device for
automatically transferring to the radio
telephone conversations originating on
metallic circuits was accomplished aft.
er extended tests conducted by direc.
ton of Captain Bullard, chief of the
navy's radio service, in cooperation
with the American Telephone and
Telegraph Company and the Western
Electric Company


President Theodore N. Vail and
other officials of the American Tele-
phone and Telegraph Company at New
York, conversed for several minutes
in clear, distinct tone, with the Mare
Island station, the conversation being
transmitted over an ordinary metallic
line from New York TO Arlington, and
thence by radio across the continent.

now visiting the sea coasts in both the
North sea and the Baltic, and the fish
ermen are making enormous catches
The fish are entering the Baltic through
the Cattegat in great shoals. and the
Danes are also taking their part in the
catch. The German fishermen are TAX
ing enormous hauls in the waters
around Kiel, Eckenfoerde and Feb
maran. and many shiploads Of ice are
coming down from Denmark and Nor
way for packing the fish for shipment
into the interior.

friends.

Washington, Sept. 8.-President
Wilson and Secretary of State Lansing
tucked away their documents and
notes on the undersea warfare, the
Dumba incident and other perplexing
international problems in their re-
spective desks this afternoon and went
out to a ball game. For the eighteen
innings of two games they forgot there
were such countries as Germany and
Austria, or that there had ever been
steamships called the Hesperian, the
Arabic and the Lusitania.


The games were for the benett OF
the fund to entertain the Grand Army
of the Republic veterans in their en-
campment here, beginning September
81. The first was between the Agri-
cultural and Interior departments,
while in the second the st. Theresas
and the Railroad Young Mems Chris
tian Association battled for suprem-
acy.


The President was in fine spirits,
throwing the ball out at the beginning
Of the game. With him and the Sec.
retary of State was also Secretary OF
the Interior Lane, who is much con-
suited on the international situation.
The French Ambassador was also
among the rooters, but he did not JOIN
the Presidential party.

have made another raid over London
dropping bombs. Eight persons arc

The Home Office soon after midnight.

Louise Mainland, a little girl, ten
wears old, and her brother, Albert
fifteen. have lived for three weeks in
a tent on Lawrence Beach, Long Island
where the only sounds are the pound

trees.

Mainland, who is said to be suffrage

healthy life for her children. AT in
tervals she would bring them food.


They lived comparatively comfort
