DOVER. November 1S-The hospital
ship Anglia, with about 300 wounded
men aboard in addition to the crew,
nurses and attendants. bound from
France for Dover, struck a mine in
midchannel and sank in a very short
time yesterday. Nearly 100 men. most
of them seriously wounded and there
fore in cots, lost their lives.


The collier Lusitania, which was
nearby at the time of the accident, i'm
mediately went to the assistance of
the Anglia. and her boats had just been
lowered when she also struck a mine
and foundered. All her crew were
saved.


A patrol vessel succeeded in rescuing
300 Of the Anglia's passengers and crew,
including some nurses. A. number of
bodies were recovered.


Official Statement.


The following official communication
concerning the disaster was made pub
lie:


The war Office reports that the hos
pital ship Anglia struck a mine in the
channel and sank. The total number
on board was 13 officers and 372 men of





saved by patrol vessel.


Another ship proceeding to the res
cue was also sunk by another NINE"
Another official communication says:
king George was shocked to hear
that the Anglia, which SO recently
conveyed him across the. channel. has
been sunk. His majesty is grieved at
the loss incurred. but trusts that the
survivors have not unduly suffered
from their terrible exposure"
Causes Anxiety in England.


The sinking of the Anglia, although
the first case in the war of a hospital
ship meeting disaster while carrying
wounded. has caused great anxiety in
the public mind. as it had been sup
posed that the English channel was en-
tirely free of danger from mines.


The newspapers indulge in much
speculation. some of them offering the
explanation that they must have been
German mines. The Anglia had 200 cot
cases aboard. When the rescuing ves-
sells reached her she was badly down
by the head and her propellers were
racing. Her stern was so high above
the sea that one of the rescuing ves-
sells was able to pass under her and
forty men dropped aboard.





narratives of this disaster. according
to which, after terrific explosion, the
bows of the Anglia seemed to melt
away until the sea Tapped her rails.
She surged forward, however, in a
vain attempt to reach shore.


y, Many Boats to Rescue.
Soon many boats came to the rescue,
including those sent by the Lusitania.
Those watching the scene saw the SOL
diers coming up from below, assem-
bling on deck and calmly waiting the
order to pass into the boats


A rescuing vessel ran right under the
sinking steamers stern, and imme-
diately the crew set to work under
greatest difficulties to transfer the
wounded.


Every moment the stern of the doomed
vessel rose higher, and the hull veered
sideways as though about to turn tur-
tie, but still the crew worked on.


Wounded Fall Into Sea.


Some of the wounded, unable to keep
their footing on the sloping deck, fell
into the sea and were picked up by the
rescuers. Others jumped overheard.
All the while the nurses worked with
splendid devotion with the crew to
transfer their patients to the boats.


The difficulties were augmented by
the racing propeller. which gave a cir
cular motion to the Anglia.


The end came with dramatic sudden
ness. With wounded soldiers and doc
tors, nurses and sailors still clinging to
the stern, the vessel appeared for a
moment to stand on her bows. then
suddenly went under, but left the Red
Cross flag flying at her mast six feet
above water. marking the fatal spot.

Before the next rush of the tide whose

stepped into the pool. The struggle be-
fore her was fearful one. She could not
swim. She stumbled for footing, the water
almost to her shoulders. A huge wave
behind her curved up like green scoop,

about her neck. She became giddy, the
panorama heaved, and she was raked

chin, close, close to her mouth, which was
agonizingly strained above them. Her
footing became more and more unsteady.
The dry land was still thirty yards away.


In that stark need that keeps the brain
clear she balanced her chances, and felt
that she would never reach it. Yet over
every inch of the leaping, smashing, fright
ening space between her and the shore she
battled for her life as if she fought wolf.

hottest part of the afternoon, woman
walked along Front Street, in fatigue
that was pain. She had the sunny
street of shops almost entirely to herself.

cotton; a bare straw hat was tied down

nous telephone message which came

and when perfectly cold pour it over the
peppers in the jars until these over

chop them in pieces: measure the pulp,
place it in kettle over the fire and boil

the tomatoes in glass jars. close at once.
and set them upside down until cold. The
more the juice is pressed from tomatoes
when the jar is being filled the more
satisfactory will be the canned vegetable.

They stopped and sent forward a re-

ZURICH, Switzerland, August 10
The exports of Swiss watches in 1914
show a decrease of more than $4,000
900. as compared with the previous
year. But for the readiness with which
Swiss manufacturers have adapted
themselves to the changed conditions
their losses would have been still
greater.


Switzerlands watch export industry is
the greatest in the world. Eightyseven
per cent of all the foreign watches sold
in the various countries of the world

there were exported more than 15,0O0.-
900 watches of a total value of some
$37 100000, while less than 300, 900
watches were sold in the home market
that year; not two per cent Of the total
production.


When the war broke out the Swiss
watch industry was brought to a sudden
standstill. The manufacturers were most
pessimistic. There were no orders; there
was no money and credit was difficult
to obtain. But changes in fashion soon
helped them to circumvent the hardships.
Obviously there was no longer any mar
ket for the more expensive watches, SO
the makers turned to producing cheaper
articles especially adapted for the mill
itary.


A great trade was done in silver,
nickel and gun metal cased watches
with luminous dials, which found a
ready sale among army men. Except
ing certain towns and districts where
only expensive watches had been made,
the industry gradually, recovered from
the first depression, and there are now
fewer unemployed workmen than at

Drought followed by excessive rains in
the cotton belt during August caused
deterioration slightly more than the
August average to the growing cotton
crop. The Department of Agriculture
today announced the condition Is 69.2
per cent of normal. That is 6.1 per
cent below the July condition.


Unofficial calculations. based on gov
eminent averages for yield. condition
and acreage, place the crop at 11,s17,-
235 equivalent 5O0-pound bales. against
16,134,930 bales last year


crop slightly under 100000 bales
was forecast by the crop reporting
board from the July % condition. The
area planted this year has been officially
reported as 81, 53!,, 900 acres.


Weather Conditions Bad.


Weather conditions for the crop had
not been very favorable during the
month. Hot and generally continued
dry weather greatly retarded growth
over many portions of the belt during
the first week and but little progress
was possible, except over the northern
portion, where local rains and moder-
ate warmth favored satisfactory
growth. During the early part of the
month drought continued very gener-
ally IN lexaS ana WAS pcCoHiiHS seNeiS
over large areas.


Continued dry weather over the
greater part Of the more important
producing states prevented satisfac-
tory growth during the second week
of the month and the crop very gem
orally de.eriorated. Shedding was re-
ported in many sections and bolls were
opening prematurely in districts where
the drought prevailed. Insect pests
were reported generally less active
than usual.


Deterioration due to adverse weather
during the early weeks of the month
was arrested by good rains over much
of the central and eastern portions of
the belt during the latter part of the
month and the crop responded to the
more favorable condition. Rain was
still needed in greater part of Missis-
sippi and in some portions of Alabama.
In the western part of the belt good
growing conditions prevailed except in
Texas where the drought continued
over much of the state until the close
of the week. when the West Indian
storm brought considerable rain over
the eastern and coast districts.

Forks. Main street is bleak and desert
ed waste The cattle from the range
Craze undisturbed among its shacks.


Here the skulking coyote may gnaw his
bone in peace and howl unmolested


through the night.


The "wickedest town in America is left
in the muck of it's own evil reputation.
For a decade East Grand Forks was
the first and last and only chance in
all that part of the world for the man
who craved the flowing bowl
1t is on the Minnesota side of the Mis-
souri, river. just across from Grand Forks,
which is in North Dakota. Nearby are
Fargo and Morehead. All are towns of
considerable Importance, all are dry as
bone, and all are populated by men who
have the fiercest kinds of fiery thirsts.
East Grand Forks came into being for
the sole purpose of relieving these thirsts.
and for years it has well served its bibu-
lous destiny. Here one could go and
click a glass and still another one and
stagger homeward at any hour he liked.


The suspender drummers and fruit tree
agents, working the dry country for their
firms, always looked forward to the big
night when they reached East Grand
Forks.


The hands on the harvesting outfits
that opened the threshing season in Okla
homa in June and worked their way
northward through the hot. dry country
used to lie awake nights and brag about
how they would whop it up when they
finally struck East Grand Forks.


But. alas, Their longings and their
boastings are now in vain. There's moth
ing doing this year. boys. The shutters
are up and the lushers all gone. Local
option carried at the last election in
Crookston county and East Grand Forks
is now as dry and abandoned as the
Sahara.

To some degree ever since Napoleon
conquered Europe short men have made
history, SIR" But popular respect for
them has increased more particularly
since the japanese thrashed the Rus
slams. Now medical authorities are step
ping forward with scientific proof that
the short man has the quicker wit and
makes the better fighter, the better smoke
eater. 1t is even contended-in Boston

glands one may regulate his height TO
suit his fancies; hence, that every one OF
us. if we had been taken in time, might
have become short, stocky, pugnacious
and efficient.


Within few days quarrymen IN west
ern Pennsylvania have come upon two
human skeletons, supposedly those of a
prehistoric man and his mate, the man
of giant stature, the woman small, I'M
dersized, undoubtedly of the clinging vine
variety, but typical Of her time. In those
DAYS the big man was king. With his
longer legs he outran and overlook the
little man, lowered over him and smashed
him with his club. And the little woman,
with her relatively larger brain IN
closer. more intimate touch with her
nerve centres, promptly wound her big,
british hero about her little finger.


Despite modern methods of warfare
which no longer favor the big man, de-
spite the doctors and the records of
diminutive heroes, there is enough of the
prehistoric left in both sexes to incline
us toward size in man. But this is sim
ply stupid conservatism with men, who
still regard the big man with instructive
awe. Women, on the other hand, with
that intuition which from the first has
made scientific reasoning superfiuous for
them, look upon him as the more COM
pliant, the easier to manage.


When it comes to choice of height
shall we please the doctors or the
women?

well, in 1874, though she continued
writing under her maiden name. For
several years she edited "Belgravis, a
London magazine. Her brother, SIR
Edward Braddon, was Prime Minister
of Tasmania.

For months Field Marshal Won
Hindenburg's troops have been fight
ing hard on the Dvinsk front. The
German official statement has said
at various times that the Russian
attacks before Dvinsk "were con-
tinued without the slightest sue
cess"


On the other hand, the Russian Of
ficial statement has said in prac-
tically the same language from time
to time the German attacks before
Dvinsk "were continued without the
slightest success"


Both the German and Russian
statements are true, for Dvinsk has
been captured two or three dozen
times, first by the Germans, then by
the Russians.


Newspaper readers who recollect
how Liege and the other forts
crumpled before the way of the Ger
man advance in Belgium and France
until the turn of the tide at the
Marne have wondered how Dvinsk
should not succumb to the great
guns of Germany and Austria. But
unlike the French and Belgian for
tifications, Dvinsk was not made of
concrete, stone, and steel. The Rus
sion fortress was constructed of
shifting sands, and therein lies the
secret. Gunners cannot knock to
pieces sand Notifications with the
ease that they have reduced con-
crete and steel. Projectiles are
smothered in the skillfully laid out
trenches.


The lessons of the war, upon which
Europe is spending billions of dol.
lars and millions of lives, ought to
be of value to America. The sand
fortress, erected at very little ex.
pense and holding out SO splendidly
for months, ought to be of interest
to our own national defense board
for use on our coasts should America
ever be attacked.

Dunaiec to the Strfba was about two hum

square miles of territory had been freed
of the invader. All the Russian conquests
save a thin slice of Galicia about Tarno-
pol had been regained, perhaps 100000
prisoners had been captured, and not less
than half million Russians had been put
out by death and wounds But the Russian
armies had not been enveloped or captured.


After the first disaster about the Duna-
ice the Grand Duke had been able to ex-
tricate his armies. He had defeated the
Austrians south of Przemysl and south
of Lemberg. Wherever the Russians and
Austrians fought without German partic-
ipation, the Russian superiority was still
manifest. But munitions had failed the
Russians and retreat had been inevitable.
Galicia had been lost to the Gar and the
battle for Poland was now on.


The Polish Salient


When the campaign opened the Russian
line had been fairly straight, with slight
bulge about Warsaw. After the fall of
Lemberg the front had been so bent back
that Poland was like nut between two
Jaws of a nutcracker, one jaw being East
Prussia, occupied by Hindenburg, the other
Galicia, now held by Mackensen and the
Austrians. In fact, the Russian line was
now about where it stood when the war
opened.


After the Russians had been driven
back beyond Lemberg, Mackensen, whose
main army had never gone far east of the
San, made half wheel to the north and
moved against the Warsaw-Kiev railroad.
His objective points were Cholm and Lub-
lin, in the gap between the Vistula, at
Ivangorod and the marshes south and
east of Cholm.


This was the only weak spot in the
whole Russian defensive position of the
Polish salient. Along the whole northern
side, from the Baltic TO Warsaw, the forts

Dunaiec. But the Russian rout was too
complete to permit a rally here, and the
Germans pressed on. At least one Russian
division, operating in the Dukla Pass, was
trabped and practically destroyed. But
the rest were able to make good their re-
tirement.


From the Wislok to the San the Russian
retreat slowed down and the rear guard
fighting became more effective. The de-
struction of the railroads and the bridges
slowed I'D the German advance. Reinforce
ments were hurried, to the Russians
Three weeks after the first disaster there
was apparently good reason to believe
that the Russians would save their armies,
DESPITE the heavy initial losses. They were
now approaching the third line Of defence
the line of the San, the southern end held
by the fortress Of Przemysl, which they
had captured before; the northern by the
field works about Jaroslav, that had held
back the Austrian drive in the preceding
November. II they could rally here they
would still hold most of Galicia.


At the San.


Along the San in the last days OF May
the Russians made a brave stand. Pre-
mysl held back the flood for some days,
and about the town and to the north the
Russians scored some local triumphs. But
the Germans now varied their attack. AS
the Russians had fallen back from the
Wisok they had drawn their troops out
of the Carpathian passes and back upon
the Dniester River. Now the Germans re-
inforced the Austrian troops which had
been holding the Hungarian side of the
passes, and these armies came rushing
down the Galician slopes and forced the
crossing of the Dniester east Of Przemysl.


The main Russian army about Przemysl
was now between two jaws, one made by
Mackensen's army, which had crossed the
San at Jaroslav and was moving south
and east Of Przemysl; the other made by

II was now perfectly clear that the Grand
Duke had determined to run no risk Of
pitched battle, but 10 follow the strategy
that had proved so disastrous to Napoleon
century before. The country was laid
in waste as the army retreated. The fields
were stripped, the population sent out be-
fore the troops. The Germans found only
desert.


At the precise moment when the escaps
of the Russian armies seemed assured the
Car suddenly relieved the Grand Duke,
and, sending him to the Caucasus, took
personal command. This was the most
momentous incident of the whole cam
paign, and to the Allied capitals 1t came
as disaster after all danger Of disaster
seemed to have passed. 1t was recognized
as meaning that the court intrigues had
removed a great general who had been
the victim of the lack of preparation Of
his nation but had in adversely displayed
military skill unrivalled in the whols
war on the Allied side.


The first fear that the change might
mean the retirement of Russia from the
war was promptly proved groundless. The
Gar issued solemn assurances to his AL
lies, and they realized that with his
throne at stake the Gar would not take
command merely to surrender. But would
the elimination of the Grand Duke bring
military, if not political, disaster? Would
the incompetent politicians replace the
great soldier? The question still remains
unanswered.


At Last a Russian Victory.


In the first hours of his control the
Gar was cheered by Russian victory. Far
to the south in Austrian Galicia his troops
took the offensive and once more van
pushed the Austrians, taking upward OK
10000 prisoners.


But rejoicing in Allied quarters was
soon turned TO panic. For the Berlin bull
letins promptly announced the fall Of
Wilma and new peril TO the central Rus
sian army. Moving first north and then
south, east of Wilma, the German troops,
mainly cavalry, had penetrated far to the
rear of the Russian army and were now
threatening to envelop it. They had
closed its retreat east and north, they
were threatening its single avenue of es-
cape toward the south.


Hindenburg was now plainly making his
last bid for a decision. The southern
armies had reached Pinsk The northern
armies were checked along the Dvina,
the Austrian armies were held up in Cali
cha. Already the weather was becoming
bad and the country in which he was
/ fighting was a swamp but little drained
since the time when Napoleon lost his
best troops between Pinsk and Beresina.
If the Russians escaped now, it was plain
that the weather would end the German
drive and give the Slavs a respite.


But if the central army were bagged,
with perhaps 100000 men, with the most
Of Russia's field artillery, then Russia
could hardly make good the loss and might
be eliminated when the freezing weather
made possible fresh operation. At tho
Dunajec, at the San, at the Vistula, the
Grand Duke had eluded the net, escaped
development. The Grand Duke was now
gone; could his successors follow his
example?

Berlin. Aug. 10.-A special dispatch
from Warsaw. dated August s, de-
scribes the German crossing of the
Nistula at Warsaw. This was effected
within the city itself, although the
buildings on the eastern bank of the
river were still occupied by Russians,
who. from the shelter of the houses.
could offer strong resistance to the
passage of the waterway.


The Russians and Germans had
maintained a vigorous fire across the
Vistula during Saturday. During the
whole day bullets whistled through the
streets leading to the waterfront of
the Polish capital. Nevertheless, the
Germans calmly worked their way
down the quay and occupied in force
houses and gardens commanding the
spot selected for the crossing.


This spot was just down the stream
from the railroad bridge. Pontoons
were brought up under cover of dark
ness and the crossing Of the river was
begun at daybreak. As soon as the
Russians perceived this movement they
hastily evacuated their positions and
abandoned the entire suburb of Praga,
firing the main railroad station and
houses and burning their supplies be-
fore departing.


About fifteen civilians were killed
and two hundred wounded in the street
fighting. many of them in the Jewish
quarter One shrapncl exploded over a
street car.

tuary, was decorated appropriately. At

assembled at the waiting hall in the

princes and princesses of the blood and
other members of the imperial family

then the emperor slowly made his way
from the inner part of the palace. at

fore the deity or holy presence. He

ualist attired in full religious costume

peak Of Zellenkofel

fighting all along the frontier has been

border line. The Italians are strongly
entrenched on high peaks inside their

ern roads for a distance of several miles

cally rushed his men forward to oc-
cupy Austrian positions overlooking the
routes of invasion.

Three homeless wanderers, a grand
mother, bent and gray. and her daugh-
ter and granddaughter. found a home to-
day. They we're sent to Blockley.


Death and desertion brought poverty
on the three generations, and hunger
put its mark on them as they drlfted
from shelter to shelter. The grand
mother, Mrs Catherine Becker, 81 years
old, hobbies on cane; her daughter
Mrs. Olga Jolelne, IS years old, walks
wearlly from lack of food. The only
bright eyes in the family are those of
5-year-old Helen Joleine but she. too,
could not have endured privation much
longer.


The little girl cried as her grandmother
led the way from the hot street into
the goth and Berks streets police station
shortly after midnight. In a quavering
voice Mrs. Becker asked the police for
help-a nights lodging for the three Of
them and something to eat in the morn
ing-perhaps they would go away in the
morning and could walt till then for
the food Tramping the streets had been
wearisome, and she leaned against the
rail


Something in the woman's 6ace-or
maybe 1t was the little girls blue plead
ing eyes-was compelling The police
asked for the trio's story. and a pitiable
tale they got


Mrs. Joleine's husband deserted her two
years ago. They were living on 23d street
above Montgomery avenue and were
happy, in a modest way, until them. The
blow was hard one. and the deserted
wife's mind gave way under the strain.
She was sent to the Philadelphia Hos
pital, weeping for her husband. who did
not return. Six weeks ago she was dis
charged as cured. and the little family
was reunited after a fashion. Two weeks
later Mrs. Becker's husband, a Civil War
veteran, died.. and their sole support,
his pension, stopped, she said. Mrs.
Becker didn't know where to apply for IT,


The landlord waited two months for
the rent money, which was scraped UP
a few times and then stopped. They were
evicted a week ago. Tramping the
streets, they managed to keep body and
soul together. A little charity they
found, but no work, for who needs
woman past middle age with daughter
and child?


Dr. William T. Ellis. police surgeon,
examined the trio and found them TO be
in actual need of food. After communi-
eating with the Philadelphia Hospital it
was found that they could be provided
for, and they were sent there today,
grandmother, daughter and grand
daughter.

streak, and added three more games

match.

Tho bright sea washed beneath her feet
AS IL had done of yore,
The well-remembered odor sweet,
Came through her opening door.
Again the grass his rlpened head
Bowed where her raiment swept,
Again the fog-bell told of dread,
And all the landscape wept.
Again beside the woodland bars
She found the wilding rose.
With petals fine and heart of stars
The flower our childhood knows
And there, before that blossom small.
BY its young face beguiled,
The woman saw her burden fall,
And stood little child.
She knew no more the weight of love,
No more the weight of grief,
So could the simple wild rose move,
And bring her heart relief.
She asked not where her love was gone,
Nor where her grief was fled,
But stood as at the great white throne,
Unmindful of things dead.


Anne Fields.

NEW YORK. August 25.-Detailed adj
vices received here today from King
ston, Jamaica. show that the damage
caused to the northern side of the
Island of Jamaica by the hurricane
August IL and 10 was greater than
indicated by earlier dispatches. The
terrific winds felled acres of banana
trees. destroying fully 80 per cent of
the banana crop, according to the in
formation.


The railway between Port Antonio
and Buff bay was virtually all wiped
out, and wagon roads along the coast
were destroyed, while in other sec
tons general damage to crops, build
ings. wharves, railways and roads was
reported.


Cocoanut plantations escaped with slight
damage. but coffee and pimento cultiva-
tions were seriously damaged. The
growers are reported to have already
undertaken to restore their plantations,
and another banana crop is promised
within ten months.

"lvangorods fall after the capitula-

LONDON. June 12.-Almost

Teutonic forces in their deter
mined efforts to continue their
recently successful offensive

nitted, also have been forced to
pay heavy toll for the gains made
in the past few days.


Success of Russian arms at this
Juncture of the war is considered
most timely, for the Germanic
forces will be unable to detach
large forces and send them either
to the western or Italian arenas,
as was feared during the time the
Teutonic advance was unchecked.


some Already Detached.

already have been detached from the
Galician armies and hurried to the
Isonzo front. but 1t is felt that even
more men will be needed there If Italy
keeps pressing on toward Trieste.


The latest official announcement from
Petrograd asserts that the Russians
have assumed the offensive along the
Dubysa river and in the Baltic prov
inces, and they concede the loss of
ground nowhere except along the River
Pruth in Bukowina.


Three Great Battles.





in perspective it may be divided rough
Iy into three great battles. The chief
of these was fought forty miles to the
southeast of Lemberg, where the
forces under Gen. Won Linsingen had
not only crossed the Dniester, but had
progressed twelve miles beyond, get
ting astride of the Lemberg railroad
These were the forces which the Rus

heavy loss. thus placing the river in

battles took place in the territory
between Ugartsberg and Zydachow
and along this line the Russians claim
to have repulsed the Germans, with
severe punishment,


North of both Of these areas the Ger
man check was complete.

couraged by Russian successes of the
past few days, for their attacks con-
Iinues with una abated fury. West OF
Shawl determined aggressive moves
have been made. but, according to

London, Feb. 15.-Prince Alexine

the Servian battlefelds, which are to
be exhibited here. They show in a
conclusive way the violence of the ef-
forts in which his gallant countrymen
have been engaged.


"The Daily News" representative, in
conversation with the prince yesterday,
was informed that Servia was prepared
for the Austrians again whenever they
approached the frontier, though at the
same time the Servians were at war
with Albania.


The prince was very modest concern
ing his country's achievements, but a
simple relation of facts is sufficient to
show how his land has suffered.


1--WE have been fighting literally for
our national existence" the prince
said. "For centuries our struggles with
invaders from the Orient are historic,
but for the last three years, with the
Turks, Bulgarians and Albanians and
now with the Teutonic powers, we have
been engaged in wars which | think
would have exhausted a less spirited
people at any other time than this.
For instance, the iniquities of the Aus
trian five days advance into my coun-
try when we were short of ammunition
would have filled the civilized world
with horror. The Austrian soldiery
must have been insane. The prince
showed photographs which fully con-
firmed this.


ave have lost 5000 women and chill
dren during the advance, and the pho
tographs show you how; but we ral-
lied and thoroughly routed them. You
will understand, therefore, that Servia
needs the attention and sympathy of
the great peoples Of the West"

There are sixteen sea heroes whom
the United States government wants to
honor with medals for bravery dis
played in rescuing survivors from the
steamer Volturna, which burned at
sea in October. 1913, but the officials
charged with the duty of carrying out
the will of Congress in decorating
these heroes have been unable to per-
form the task. although diligent search
has been made for them.


On October and 10. 1913. the Kroon-
lano went to the assistance of the
burning steamer Volturno in the north
Atlantic ocean and succeeded in rescu-
Ing eighty-nine persons.


Recognition of Gallantry.


For their gallant work the. Kroon-
lands officers and crew received the
thanks Of Congress. and $1,000 was APP
propriated by the above mentioned res
olution for the purchase of solid gold
watch and chain for Capt. Paul H.
kreibohm and five gold, five silver and
twenty nine bronze medals for the
other officers and the crew. Secretary
Redfield was authorized and directed to
purchase the watch and medals and to
present them.


Secretary Redfeld, with other depart
ment- officials, went to New York in
January last and presented the watch
and chain to Capt. Kreibohm, and
medals to nine of the officers and crew,
the only ones who could be located at
that time. Since then fourteen others
have been found and have received
their medals. The difficulty experienced
in locating the brave men to whom the
medals were awarded Is illustrated in
that one medal was delivered in Lon
don, England, while the recipient of
another was found in the Belgian army.

Schaub, Henri Guelinck. Emil Bohme,
Desire Auguste Coopman, Ernst
Benecke, Leon Coppens. Petrus Stob-
blelaar. Gustav Ebling, Alphons Roll
and August Friedrich Reckzugel.

sioner at New York city and the man.
ager of the International Mercantile

walked on four feet: others with small,
weak fore limbs walked entirely upon
the strongly developed hind legs. Some
had reptilelike feet; others were bird
footed. Some had toes provided with
long, sharp claws; others had fiat
tened hooflike nails.


There We're dinosaurs with small
heads and others with large heads. Some
We're large and cumbersome: others were
small light and graceful. and SO much re-
Semoled birds in their structu..e that only
the skilled ana atomist can distinguish their
remains. Some OF enormous size were
clad in coats of bony armor. which
gave them most bizarre appearance.

American Can. London's market for
Americans was extremely dull, with

Foreign Exchange Market Feature.


The event of the week, because OF
it's general bearing upon the financial
situation, was the unprecedented de-
cline in foreign exchange and its sub
sequent recovery Demand sterling
fell to $3.50, the lowest quotation ever
officially reported in this market. with

storing order to exchange markets as
whole.

outcome of the Arabic incident with
lively satisfaction, this being height
ened by later developments calculated
to make for peace among the warning
powers.

opinion in high quarters regarding the
actual state of business throughout the

With hands working, slim figure
swaying, pink cheeks and brilliant
eyes, Theresa Judd walked back and
forth across the living room floor, her
thin voice breaking into impassioned
utterances. In the next room. which
was the dining room. her daughter,
Theodosia, aged eleven, sat very still,
with her legs curled under her, ap-
parently reading.


Theresa had been thus walking
long time She had, indeed, forgotten
how long She was lost In imagina-
tion as she recited. The piece was
long and difficult, and had proved a
task to memorize, but she was sure
of it at last. All that remained for
her to do was to polish it until 1t
should be ready for presentation to
her hearers.


A great occasion awaited Theresa's
elocution. She had been asked to
speak that evening at the symposium
of the women's clubs. Westmore
prided itself on its clubs, of which
from mere tete-a-tete affair of four
or so members, which met with work

postum had been arranged with much
careful attention to details. There was
to be plenty of music. of course. But
there was only one person who could
"elocute," as Miss Preston said. And
that person was Theresa Judd.


Theresa Judd was what is called
born speaker" She had never had
any instruction other than that fond
teachers and parents and one ro-
mantle old aunt had given her. 1t had
any other. Theresa was not conccited.
She was merely ignorant She had
never in her life heard any one who
could recite the Charge of the Light
Brigade" better than she did. She had,
in fact, never been out of Westmore
more than three or four times.


Theresa loved the whole business OF
reciting. She was ever on the look
out for new pieces. When she found
one to her taste she could scarcely eat
or sleep until she had learned it. And
when she had learned it she practiced
it faithfully, it filled her with pro-
found emotion to hear the sound of
her own voice rolling off eloquent
phrases.


Now, suddenly upon her pacing and
rehearsing broke her little daughters
small. quiet voice. "Pa's coming" said
Theodosia-


Theresa stopped She had forgotten
everything save the death scene of
picturing. The facts of everyday life
flowed back upon her In slow. chill
ing tide. Tunis, her husband, was
coming home from his carpenter work,
and she had forgotten supper! She
had meant to make a pan of biscuits.

While Mounted Patrolman O'Brien,

ting his horse along the beach at

an fifty yards from shore throw up

" toward the drowning woman, while

10 the surface. An ambulance was

BERLIN. February 5.-The German
newspapers have commenced the publi-
cation of a series of eyewitness ar
ticles on naval affairs, written by Otto
Won Gottberg, well known author. Of
the battle of January "a, in which the
German cruiser Bluecher was sunk, Won
Gottberg, writing from interviews with
participants, mostly officers, says the
German squadron was made up OF the
first class cruisers Bluecher, Seydlitz,
Derff1inger and Moltke; the smaller


cruisers Kolberg. Stralsund. Graudenz
and Rostock, of which the last two were
not engaged In the actual fighting, and
torpedo craft.


The Kolberg was the first to sight the
enemy, small British cruiser, accom-
panied by destroyers. The remainder of
the British fleet was still below the


horizon. The Kolberg Immediately
opened fire.


Artillery Duel Begins.
After several minutes the British ship
opened with one of her forward guns
and then began an artillery duel between
the two small cruisers.


The Kolberg noted that several OF


her shells made good hits. The hol-


berg received two British shots. one
from a 15-centimeter (6-inch) gun and


the other from a 1O.2-centimeter four-
inch). Neither shot did much mate
rial damage, but three men were killed
and two were wounded.


The Kolberg steamed ahead, and was
planning to close with the enemy
However, her sister cruiser. the stral-
sund, steaming farther to the right and
a long distance ahead of the squadron


had sighted the main body of the Brit
cio
admiral, on board the Seydlitz. Eight
large hostile ships sighted on starboard
bow"
The British ships again dropped out


some time later, when the pilot of the
Moltke called attention to hVe DIG
ships on the starboard quarter, that Is.
to the westward, on the opposite SIDE
from those seen before.


Big Shell Unmasks Enemy.


"The commander and the pilot


writes Won Gottberg. were still study
ing through their glasses the five
scarcely visible shadows on the gray
waves when a big shell struck the wa
ter 500 yards away. throwing up high


pillar of water. The enemy had un-
masked himself. Either five hitherto


unreported big ships had been lurking


undiscovered behind our ships, or else
five of the eight previously sighted had
made wide circuits completely around our
squadron.


"The German ships Immediately an
swered the fire of the enemy. In or
der to bring more guns into action.
first the enemy. then the German
squadron took the familiar echelon
formation, like a flight of steps, and
steamed along twenty-five kiiometers
(thirteen miles) apart, each snip try
ing by constant turning to bring as
many guns as possible to bear. Inc
British concentrated their fire on our
rearmost ship, the Bluecher, and short
ly landed a. severe hit over the engine
room. THIS forced the Bluecher to
drop back slowly even before she
hoisted her last signal after second
shot reached the engine room: All en-
gines useless


from forebridge to stern. the pillar OF
fire above her towering to the sky.
"Forty-fve minutes later the quar-
terdeck of the S:eydlitz also began to
blaze The Seydlitz. of all the ships
which returned. was the only one on
which the two-hour bombardment in
fiicted any real injury.


THE damage to the whole squadron.
in fact, was so slight that the admiral
did not need to dock a single ship.
They are all at this moment ready to
run out against the enemy. The patch
ing of the Seydlitz's turret is being
done rapidly, and will take at the most
only a few days.

GENEVA, March 4.-The first train
load Of MANNED German prisoners of
war, who are to be exchanged for
wounded French soldiers, arrived here
from Lyons. homeward bound. The spe-
cial glided into the station between
lanes of Swiss troops.

by Red Cross nurses. who distributed
gifts Of oranges. chocolate and other
delicacies among the sufferers. relieving
their French co-workers of the RESPONSE
bility of caring for the passengers.


Swiss government physicians went
rapidly through the train. but found that
none of the 240 Germans aboard re-
quired medical attention.


All Of them seemed cheerful and con-
tented They accepted gratefully the
gifts showered upon them.


There was no demonstration, as the
public was excluded from the station.


Most of the Germans had been Grip
pied by the loss of leg or an arm and
many of them had lost two limbs. Most
Of them were smoking cigarettes.


They paid tribute to the kind treat
ment they had received in French hos
pitals. After long stop, the train left
for Schaffhausen. at the northernmost
point in Switzerland. where it will pass
the train carrying incapacitated French
prisoners on their way home.

close the place of capture nor detail
the circumstances He said. however.

largest type in the German navy, and
that the craft carried a double crew.

manned all of the large submarines

the people of Ohio had general election to elect

while this year prohibition was the principal issue
The prohibitionists last year complained that


there was trading against them in connection with
the State ticket. They have no excuse for that
complaint this year. They made the issue, claimed
they had better organization than before


and that they had large campaign fund. They

only substantial gains they made were in Cincin-
natl and Cleveland, where the vote was still four
to and two to one against them.

cause of prohibition refrigerated in Ohio in the

Medical Observers send reports, like
passages from Dante, describing the tor
lures of the damned.


Carloads of shrieking men, with their
backbones arched forward like bows, in
the rigors of lockjaw.


Hospitals full of soldiers bloated like
balloons, in awful agony.


Horrors the prophets never dreamed
of, these.


Yet their cause is perfectly clear.


They are Natures punishment for the
crime of fighting over plowed ground.


The soil upon which men have lived
and in which they have delved for CEN
turies Is where the tetanus bacillus that
causes lockjaw lives and dourishes.


It isn't even safe to walk barefoot over
country like that.


Every bullet that carries with it into
soldiers body bit Of his uniform
stained with this rich soil carries poten-
tial death in its most horrible form, no
matter how slight the actual wound


And the gas germs, too, come out OF
the soil-the soil Of the most fertile. in
tensely cultivated farm lands in the
world, the fields of France and Belgium.


The same nitrogen-gathering bacteria
that gave these fair acres their richness
now bloat men into the size Of two men.


Science may, and doubtless will, con-
quer these new horrors of war.


DIR. Meltzser of the Rockefeller Insti-
tute for Medical Research has invented
an apparatus that makes the admins
tration of anti-tetanus serum easier and
safer, and they are rushing these
machines over to the battle grounds as
fast as the American manufacturers can
make them.


But who will find slayer Of the gas
germ. which makes a man bigger than
the bed he lies on?

Several hundred persons lined the

been worth millions to movie COM
pany. Down the stream swept launch,

ately to turn the head of the craft
toward shore. The paddle snapped in

worn down the German powers of
resistance in the Champagne
region. according to dispatches re-
ceived here today. The German
second line trenches are crumbling
under the heavy pounding of shells
and there are indications that the
enemy's line is about to give way
along a wide front.


The capture of Tahure and the
Tahure heights, reported in last
nights communique, was accom-
plished with comparatively slight
losses for hte French. French guns
blotted out the German redoubts
and trenches and leveled a few
stone buildings concealing enemy
guns. A few infantry regiments
stormed the remaining works and
bayonetted the German occupants.


The victory at Failure was one
Of the most important successes
gained by the French since the in
itial drive in the Champagne swept
the enemy out Of his first line The
ease with which IL was accom-
plished convinced military men here
that the Bazaincourt- t-Challerange
railway, now less than two miles
from the French advanced works,
will be pierced within the next fort
night OF hghting, perhaps before.

The battleship Connecticut left Port

Secretary Daniels announced today.

American naval forces from Haiti.
Rear Admiral Caperton remains in
command of the American forces in

The Connecticut was sent south with
a big force of marines when landing
parties from the Washington encoun-
tered opposition after orders to take

The Washingtons marines and blue
Jackets relieved marines from the
French cruiser Des Cartes, landed to

Prince after the assassination of the
late President Guillaume of the island

the Atlantic fleet after overhaul.


Secretary Daniels said that with the
restoration of order under the new
government in Haiti and the rati'lca-

land governments finances for ten
years. the naval forces would be with
drawn gradually. No marines from the
landing force have been Withdrawn as
yet, however, the Connecticut bringing
only the 800 men of her own crew.


New Treaty in Operation.


The new Haitian treaty, by which the
United States extends broad financial
protectorate over the island republic
now is in operation under modus vi
vendi which has been signed by the
American minister and the Haitian sec
retary Of foreign affairs. This tenn
porary arrangement will continue until
the United States Senate has an oppor-
tunity to consider the treaty, which al
ready has been ratified by the Haitian
government.


The treaty goes further in giving
the United States control over Haiti's
finances than does the convention un-
der which the United States collects
and supervises the customs receipts
in the Dominican republic. Under the
| latter arrangement the United States
| retains a portion of the receipts for
payment of foreign creditors and the
cans. Under the Haitian agreement,
| however. Haiti agrees that the agents
| of the United States are to retain a
| measure of control not only over the

| creditors but also over the funds to

LONDON, January 2o.-Ger-
man airmen delivered their long
predicted attack on England last
night.


From a base presumably in
Germany they flew over the
North Sea to the eastern coast OF
England where, for nearly four
hours, from $40 pm. until about
midnight, they circled over
group of some six English towns
only little more than 100 miles
from London. apparently drop
ping bombs at will.


So far as has been learned to-
day four or five persons were
killed by these missiles and about
as many more were wounded.


All Raiders Probably Escaped.


Whether these airships were Zeppelin
dirigible balloons or aeroplanes has not
yet definitely been established. There
Is increasing belief in London this
morning that possibly only aeroplanes
took part In the attack.


There has been no news SO far today
to confirm the report current last night
that Zeppelin had been brought down
on the English coast; on the contrary.
1t now appears as though all the Ger
man raiders have returned whence
they came


The most important towns over which
the German airmen appeared were
Sandringham. Yarmouth, Sheeringham.
Hunstanton, Cromer. Heacham, Der
singh and Kings Lynn.


Close Behind the King.


King George had left Sandringham
only a few hours before the Germans
visited it, Most of the damage appears
to have been inflicted upon private
houses and shops; few public buildings
or docks seem to have been injured.


The raiding airmen showed excellent
ability to pilot their vessels. we'll as
good craftsmanship. In spite of the
darkness of the night they seemed to
find their way over the country with
remarkable directness. and the accu-
racy of their aim with bombs was
greater than generally had been be-
lieved possible.

SAN DIEGO, Cal. May 1.-Eleven
members of the crew Of the steamship
Victoria. which foundered off the
Coronado Islands late Friday, were
picked up by the schooner Flyer today
on it's way to their rescue. They had
taken to the lifeboats shortly before
the Victoria sank.


The men chose to remain on the leak
ing vessel. hoping to save her, when
the eleven passengers were taken off
last night by the American -Hawa iian
steamer American.


The men suffered from exhaustion
and exposure during their voyage in
the open boats. but none was in a
serious condition.

SAN FRANCISCO. May 1.-The
Pacific coast. storm which sent the
steamer Victoria to the bottom dis
abled the liner Northern Pacific, dam
aged the passenger steamer Harvard
and kept scores Of vessels, big and lit
tie. OFT at sea for many hours, had sub
sided tonight.


Two big steamers. the Pennsylvania
and J. L. Luckenbach, and a stream OF
small craft have come into port.


The Northern Pacific, which, with $50
passengers aboard, had been drifting
before the storm off Point Arena, 100
miles north of here, sent word late to-
day that the steam steering gear,
which had been disabled, had been re-
paired and she was expected to come
into port under her own power. The
United States coast guard cutter Nc
Culioch, tugs Defiance and IaQua and
tanker Col. E. L. Drake went to her as
sistance during the day.


Fear for the Aggi.


Anxiety is being felt regarding the
Norwegian ship Aggi, which left here
Thursday in tow Of the steamer Edgar
H. Vance. Yesterday. during the storm,
the towing line broke, and since then
the Aggi has been adrift and no word
today, reported her position as llO
miles west Of Point Arena, returning to
port. She has notified all shipping to
keep watch for the Aggi.


The Hawaiian freighter
Iowan. from New York, reported she
would reach port tonight.


Reports tonight indicated that the
damage to the fruit crop, feared as a
result of the Storm had not material
lied.


Admiral Howard, commanding the
Pacific fleet, was directed yesterday to
send a vessel to Guadalupe Island,
OFF the Mexican coast. 300 miles south
Of San Diego, Cal, to rescue five San
Francisco citizens. shipwrecked and
marooned on the island. No details
of the shipwreck were given by Sen
ator-elect Phelan of California, who
made the request.

At the end of the fifth month of the European
war the deadlock on the two fronts is still more
or less nbroken. In the west operations de-
generated many weeks ago into mere trench
warfare. The German offensive directed against
Dunkirk and Calais failed, with great loss, about
the end of November, and since then the Allies
have made slight gains all along the western line
But the French and British forces are still fol
lowing a waiting policy, and it looks as if their
real offensive will not be developed until con-
siderable portion of the new British army is
available. Germany still holds Belgium and
segment of Northeastern France but after five
heart-breakng months the famboyant hopes with
which Berlin began the war in this quarter have
faded into nothingness.


In the eastern theatre strategy is still a con-
trolling factor, and the eastern campaigns have
been brilliant demonstration Of big scale gen
eralship. Germany has become committed to
lavish use Of men on this front the political
necessity Of succoring Austra-Hungary having
spoiled the original German plan of merely con
tanning Russia ON the east until decisive success
had been won in the west against the French and
British Field Marshal Won Hindenburg has sue
ceeded i'm keeping Prussan territory practically
clear Of the enemy He has even carried the war
into the interior Of Poland and has the Russian
armies Of the centre crowded back on the line
Of the Nistula. But the Austro-Hmgarian
armies have more o, less broken down trying TO
keep pace with Won Hindenburg's offensive. This


lure has been the most important military de-
yelopment on the eastern front.


Austria Hungary has gotten the worst Of it in
every Joint strategic movement Her forces in
the north took the offensive three times in con-
formity with German plans Each time they
were severely handled and had to abandon more
territory TO the Russians. They have also been
driven twice out of Servia. the second disaster
being precptated by the diversion of troops to
Northern Hungary for the purpose of taking part
in the last joint campaign against Warsaw
Austria Hungary is the weak spot in the Teutonic
alliance, and the Russians have therefore shown
good military judgment in centring their main
effort on the campaign for Cracow.


Russia has been the surprise Of the war so far.
Germans exceptional military efficiency had long
been recognized. The high soldiery quality of
the French has never been disputed. The value
Of Great Britans small standing army was
known. Servia's forttude had been tested and
Austria-Hungary's relative weakness had been
foreshadowed But RuSsas capacity was in
doubt. Five months Of the great war have now
wiped out the memories of the Manchurian cam,
paign and sody re-ectabshed the profession !
ability of the Russian officer and the reputa-
ton Of the Russian soldier for willingness, disci-
rline and endurance.

neys and roofs were damaged by wind
